name: Ottoman Empire
summary: Founded c. 1299 by Osman I as a frontier principality in northwest Anatolia, the Ottoman state crossed into the Balkans, took Constantinople in 1453 and under Selim I and Suleiman I absorbed the Mamluk lands and most of Hungary. It reached its greatest extent around 1683, then lost ground to Habsburg Austria, Russia and Balkan nationalism over two centuries, and was dismantled after defeat in the First World War; the sultanate was abolished in 1922.

events.text: Orhan takes Bursa, which becomes the Ottoman capital
events.detail: The Ottomans began as a small Turkish frontier principality in northwest Anatolia, on the edge of the shrinking Byzantine Empire. Orhan, son of the founder Osman I, first took Mudanya, the port linking the wealthy Byzantine city of Bursa (ancient Prusa) to the Sea of Marmara, and in 1326 Bursa itself fell after its commander was persuaded to change sides. Bursa became the first real Ottoman capital, with the first Ottoman mint, new mosques and markets, and a thriving silk trade. Owning a major city helped turn a raiding beylik into a state; the capital moved on to Edirne, in Europe, in the 1360s.

events.text: Victory over a Serbian-led coalition at Kosovo
events.detail: By the 1380s the Ottomans had crossed into Europe and were pressing on the Serbian principalities left divided after the death of Emperor Stefan Dušan. On 15 June 1389 Sultan Murad I met an army led by Prince Lazar of Serbia, with Bosnian troops and other allies, on the Kosovo field near modern Pristina. Much of both armies was destroyed and both leaders were killed; Murad's death is traditionally credited to the knight Miloš Obilić. Reliable accounts are scarce and early reports even disagreed on who had won, but Serbia could no longer raise large armies, and its princes became Ottoman vassals in the following years.

events.text: Timur defeats and captures Bayezid I at Ankara; civil war to 1413
events.detail: Sultan Bayezid I had built an empire from the Danube to eastern Anatolia and was blockading Constantinople when he clashed with Timur, the Turco-Mongol conqueror of Central Asia and Persia. On 28 July 1402 the two armies met on the Çubuk plain near Ankara; Timur's larger, mostly cavalry force, perhaps 140,000 strong against no more than 85,000, won decisively after troops from the Anatolian beyliks deserted Bayezid. The sultan was captured and died in captivity months later. His sons then fought a civil war, the Ottoman Interregnum, until Mehmed I defeated his last rival at Çamurlu in 1413 and reunited the state.

events.text: Mehmed II conquers Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire
events.detail: By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was little more than its capital, Constantinople, surrounded by Ottoman lands in Europe and Asia. The young Sultan Mehmed II besieged it from 6 April with an army that far outnumbered the defenders, and with giant cannons that blasted gaps in the ancient Theodosian walls. After 53 days the city fell on 29 May, and the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in its fall. Mehmed made Constantinople (Istanbul) his capital in place of Edirne and styled himself Caesar of the Romans. The conquest joined the empire's Anatolian and Balkan halves around a single imperial city, and is often taken as the end of the Middle Ages.

events.text: Selim I defeats Safavid Shah Ismail at Chaldiran
events.detail: The Shia Safavid dynasty under Shah Ismail I had won a fervent following among the Turkmen Qizilbash tribes of eastern Anatolia, a direct threat to the Sunni Ottomans. Sultan Selim I marched east, and on 23 August 1514 his army, estimated at 60,000 to 100,000 with heavy artillery and musket-armed Janissaries behind a barrier of carts, crushed Ismail's cavalry at Chaldiran in northwest Iran. Ismail was wounded and the Safavid capital, Tabriz, was briefly occupied. The Ottomans annexed eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia, halting Safavid expansion to the west and opening 41 years of war that ended only with the Peace of Amasya in 1555.

events.text: Mamluk Sultanate annexed: Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz become Ottoman
events.detail: After Chaldiran, Selim I turned on the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and Syria, a rival for the spice trade and for leadership of the Muslim world. On 24 August 1516 his army routed the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq, north of Aleppo, where Sultan al-Ghawri was killed, and on 24 January 1517 it won again at Ridaniya outside Cairo. The last Mamluk sultan, Tuman Bay, was captured and hanged at a gate of Cairo, and the Sharif of Mecca accepted Ottoman overlordship. Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, became Ottoman, turning a mainly Anatolian and Balkan state into an empire spanning the traditional heartlands of Islam.

events.text: Suleiman I crushes Hungary at Mohács
events.detail: Suleiman I took Belgrade in 1521, opening the road into the Kingdom of Hungary, which was weakened by quarrelling nobles and a weak monarchy. On 29 August 1526 his army, with the grand vizier Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha, met the Hungarian royal army near Mohács on the Danube. The Hungarians charged too early and were encircled and destroyed by Ottoman troops and artillery; the young King Louis II drowned in a marshy stream while fleeing, and much of the nobility died. Hungary was left without a king or army, and by 1541 it was divided between the Ottomans, the Habsburgs and an eastern kingdom under Ottoman protection.

events.text: Conquest of Crete completed after the long Cretan War
events.detail: Crete was the largest and richest overseas possession of the Republic of Venice. The Ottomans invaded in 1645 and quickly overran most of the island, but the fortified capital, Candia (modern Heraklion), held out in a siege that began in 1648 and lasted more than twenty years, supplied by sea with help from France, the Papacy and the Knights of Malta. A final great expedition under Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed broke Venetian resistance, and Candia surrendered on 5 September 1669. Venice kept only a few island fortresses off the coast, and Crete remained Ottoman until it became autonomous in 1897.

events.text: Second siege of Vienna fails; the empire is at its greatest extent
events.detail: Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha, hoping to succeed where Suleiman had failed in 1529, besieged the Habsburg capital of Vienna in the summer of 1683. After two months the city was close to falling, but on 12 September a relief army of Imperial German and Polish troops under King John III Sobieski of Poland attacked from the Kahlenberg heights and routed the besiegers. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade on 25 December for the defeat. The empire was then at or near its greatest extent, but the failure opened the Great Turkish War against a Holy League of Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia, and Vienna was never besieged again.

events.text: Treaty of Karlowitz: Hungary and Transylvania lost to the Habsburgs
events.detail: The Great Turkish War that followed the defeat at Vienna went badly for the Ottomans, ending in a crushing defeat by the Habsburg army at Zenta in 1697. At Karlowitz (Sremski Karlovci, in today's Serbia) the sultan signed peace with the Holy League on 26 January 1699, each side keeping the land it held. The Habsburgs gained most of Hungary, Croatia and Slavonia, with Transylvania under Austrian governors; Poland recovered Podolia; and Venice took the Morea (Peloponnese) and most of Dalmatia. It was the first major Ottoman loss of territory in Europe, reversing almost four centuries of expansion and making the Habsburgs the leading power in the region.

events.text: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca after defeat by Russia; Crimea made nominally independent
events.detail: Russia under Catherine II went to war with the Ottomans in 1768 and won a series of victories on land and sea. The peace signed at Küçük Kaynarca (now Kaynardzha in Bulgaria) on 21 July 1774 forced the sultan to recognise the Tatars of the Crimean Khanate, an Ottoman vassal, as independent; in practice the khanate depended on Russia, which annexed it in 1783. Russia also gained Azov, Kerch and land at the mouth of the Dnieper, giving it outlets to the Black Sea, plus the right to speak for Orthodox Christians in the empire. The Black Sea was no longer an Ottoman lake, and the Crimea was the first Muslim land the sultans lost.

events.text: Greek independence formally recognised
events.detail: The Greeks rose against Ottoman rule in 1821. Britain, France and Russia intervened, destroying the Ottoman fleet at Navarino in 1827, and Russia's victory in the war of 1828–29 forced the sultan to accept the Treaty of Adrianople. On 3 February 1830 the three powers signed the London Protocol, the first international act recognising Greece as a fully independent, sovereign state, with a northern border running from the mouth of the Achelous river to the mouth of the Spercheios. In 1832 the small new Kingdom of Greece received Prince Otto of Bavaria as king. It was the first Balkan nation to break away completely from the empire.

events.text: Congress of Berlin confirms heavy losses in the Balkans
events.detail: In 1877–78 Russia defeated the Ottomans again and, by the Treaty of San Stefano, created a large Russian-aligned Bulgaria reaching the Aegean. Britain and Austria-Hungary objected, and Europe's great powers met in Berlin, with Otto von Bismarck as mediator, from 13 June to 13 July 1878. The Treaty of Berlin cut back Bulgaria and returned Macedonia to the sultan, but it recognised the full independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania, made Bulgaria an autonomous principality and Eastern Rumelia a self-governing province, let Austria-Hungary occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina, and gave Britain Cyprus. The empire lost direct control of much of its Balkan land.

events.text: Balkan Wars (1912–13) strip away almost all remaining European land
events.detail: In 1912 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro formed the Balkan League to drive the Ottomans out of Macedonia and Thrace, where many of their own peoples still lived. The First Balkan War began on 8 October 1912; within weeks the League's armies had overrun Macedonia and Albania, and Bulgarian forces were stopped only at the Çatalca line outside Istanbul. By the Treaty of London (30 May 1913) the empire gave up almost everything in Europe, and Albania became independent. In the Second Balkan War the allies turned on Bulgaria, and the Ottomans regained Edirne, but only Eastern Thrace remained of nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule in Europe.

events.text: Sultanate abolished on 1 November; the Ottoman state ends
events.detail: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on Germany's side in 1914; after its defeat, Allied troops occupied Istanbul and treaties carved up its lands. A Turkish national movement led by Mustafa Kemal (later Atatürk) set up a Grand National Assembly in Ankara in 1920 and won the War of Independence. On 1 November 1922 the Assembly abolished the sultanate, ending an empire that had lasted since about 1299, and the last sultan, Mehmed VI, left Istanbul on the British warship HMS Malaya on 17 November. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, and the caliphate was abolished in March 1924.

name: Ming China
summary: The Hongwu Emperor proclaimed the Ming in 1368 after driving out the Mongol Yuan, and his successors pushed into Yunnan, Manchuria and, briefly, Vietnam, while Zheng He's fleets sailed to the Indian Ocean. After the Tumu disaster of 1449 the dynasty turned defensive behind the rebuilt Great Wall; fiscal crisis, rebellion and the rising Manchus brought the fall of Beijing in 1644, and Ming loyalist courts in the south held out until 1662.

events.text: Ming armies annex the southwest (Yunnan), former Dali lands
events.detail: Yunnan in the far southwest had been the Dali kingdom until the Mongols conquered it in the 1250s, and it was still held for the Mongol Northern Yuan by the Prince of Liang, Basalawarmi, after the Ming took the rest of China. In 1381 the Hongwu Emperor sent a large army under Fu Youde, Lan Yu and Mu Ying. The Ming forces overwhelmed the Yuan loyalists, Basalawarmi killed himself in January 1382, and the old Dali realm of the Duan family was crushed by early 1383. Mu Ying's troops stayed on as hereditary garrisons, binding Yunnan firmly to China, where it has remained.

events.text: Campaign against Naghachu ends with Ming control of Manchuria
events.detail: After the Mongols were driven from China in 1368, the Mongol commander Naghachu still held much of southern Manchuria with a large army, threatening the Ming's northeastern frontier. In 1387 the Hongwu Emperor sent a huge force under Feng Sheng, Fu Youde and Lan Yu, and a mix of military pressure and diplomacy persuaded Naghachu to surrender. He and thousands of his officers and relatives were sent to Nanjing, where he was given a noble title and estates. The surrender removed the last Yuan stronghold in the region and brought southern Manchuria under Ming control.

events.text: Yongle Emperor seizes the throne after the Jingnan campaign
events.detail: The founder Hongwu had made his grandson emperor, but his son Zhu Di, the Prince of Yan, commanded the frontier armies at Beiping (Beijing). When the young Jianwen Emperor tried to cut back the princes' power, Zhu Di rebelled in 1399, calling his revolt the Jingnan ('pacifying the troubles') campaign. After three years of civil war his army crossed the Yangtze and took the capital, Nanjing, in 1402; the palace burned and Jianwen disappeared, probably dying in the fire. Zhu Di took the throne as the Yongle Emperor. He launched the dynasty's most ambitious period of expansion, overseas voyages and great building projects.

events.text: Zheng He's first treasure-fleet voyage sets out
events.detail: The Yongle Emperor wanted to display Ming power and bring foreign rulers into China's tribute system. In 1405 the court eunuch Zheng He, a Muslim from Yunnan, set sail from Nanjing with, according to Ming records, 317 ships, including some 62 giant 'treasure ships', and about 27,800 men. Between 1405 and 1433 seven voyages reached Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, Arabia and the east coast of Africa. Dozens of states sent envoys and tribute in return. The voyages stopped after 1433 and were never resumed; the Ming turned to defending its northern frontier, and its influence at sea faded.

events.text: Ming invasion and occupation of Đại Việt (Vietnam) begins
events.detail: In 1400 the minister Hồ Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty of Đại Việt (northern Vietnam). The Yongle Emperor used the coup as a reason to intervene, claiming to restore the Trần, and in late 1406 two large Ming armies invaded from Guangxi and Yunnan. By mid-1407 they had captured Hồ Quý Ly and his sons and taken the country. Instead of restoring the old dynasty, the Ming annexed Đại Việt as the province of Jiaozhi, the first Chinese rule there since the 10th century. The occupation pushed the empire's southern frontier deep into Vietnam, but it faced constant revolts.

events.text: Beijing designated the capital in place of Nanjing
events.detail: Since 1368 the Ming capital had been Nanjing, on the Yangtze. The Yongle Emperor had built his power in the north as Prince of Yan at Beiping, and he wanted to rule close to the Mongol frontier. From 1406 he had the city rebuilt on a vast scale, with the palace complex later known as the Forbidden City, and the Grand Canal was restored to carry grain north. In 1420 Beijing ('northern capital') was formally made the main capital, with Nanjing as a secondary one. Beijing has remained China's capital for most of the time since, and the move placed the court close to the dangerous northern border.

events.text: Ming troops withdraw from Vietnam after Lê Lợi's war
events.detail: The Ming occupation of Vietnam was harsh, with heavy taxes, forced labour and efforts to spread Chinese culture. In 1418 the landowner Lê Lợi began a rising in Thanh Hóa, using guerrilla tactics in the hills. By 1426 his forces had defeated Ming armies and were besieging the capital, Đông Quan (Hanoi), and in 1427 they destroyed a large Ming relief army at Chi Lăng. The Ming commander swore to withdraw, and his army left at the end of 1427. Lê Lợi founded the Later Lê dynasty, Vietnam became independent again, and the Ming empire's southern frontier went back to roughly its old line.

events.text: Tumu Crisis: the Zhengtong Emperor captured by the Oirats
events.detail: The Oirat Mongols under Esen Taishi had united the steppe and raided the Ming frontier in 1449 after a dispute over trade. The young Zhengtong Emperor, urged on by his eunuch adviser Wang Zhen, led a large but poorly prepared army out of Beijing. On its way back the army was caught at the post station of Tumu and destroyed in September 1449; Wang Zhen was killed and the emperor taken prisoner. The court quickly put his brother on the throne as the Jingtai Emperor, and the minister Yu Qian defended Beijing. The disaster ended Ming offensives into the steppe, and the dynasty turned to building walls along the north.

events.text: Japanese invasion of Korea; Ming armies intervene (Imjin War, to 1598)
events.detail: In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had just unified Japan, sent a huge army into Korea, a Ming tributary, as the first step toward conquering China. The Japanese took Seoul and Pyongyang within weeks, while the Korean navy under Admiral Yi Sun-sin attacked their supply lines at sea. Ming armies crossed the Yalu River and retook Pyongyang in 1593, and peace talks failed. Japan invaded again in 1597, but after Hideyoshi's death in 1598 its forces withdrew. Korea was saved and stayed a Ming ally, but the long war drained the Ming treasury just as a new threat grew in Manchuria.

events.text: Manchu Later Jin defeat a large Ming army at Sarhu
events.detail: Nurhaci, a Jurchen chieftain, had united many Jurchen tribes and in 1616 proclaimed the Later Jin state, then in 1618 declared war on the Ming. In spring 1619 the Ming sent a large army, with Korean and Yehe allies, in four separate columns to destroy him. Nurhaci concentrated his banner troops and defeated the columns one by one around Sarhu, in today's Liaoning, over a few days. Ming losses were very heavy. The battle gave the Jurchens the initiative in the northeast; within a few years they took Shenyang and Liaoyang, and the Ming lost most of Liaodong.

events.text: Li Zicheng takes Beijing; the Chongzhen Emperor dies by suicide
events.detail: In the 1630s and 1640s famine, epidemics and heavy taxes drove huge peasant rebellions in northern China, while the best Ming armies were tied down against the Manchus. The rebel leader Li Zicheng proclaimed his own Shun dynasty at Xi'an and marched on Beijing, which he entered almost unopposed in April 1644. On 25 April the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on a hill behind the palace, ending Ming rule in the north. Li held the capital for little more than a month. The Ming general Wu Sangui joined the Manchus at Shanhai Pass, and the Qing took Beijing in June, beginning their conquest of China.

events.text: Qing forces take Nanjing; the Hongguang court collapses
events.detail: After Beijing fell, Ming loyalists in Nanjing put the Prince of Fu on the throne as the Hongguang Emperor, the first of the Southern Ming rulers. His court was divided by factions, and its generals quarrelled. In 1645 Qing armies under Prince Dodo swept south, took Yangzhou after a brief siege and massacred many of its people, then crossed the Yangtze. Nanjing surrendered in June 1645 without a fight, and the Hongguang Emperor was captured and taken to Beijing, where he was executed in 1646. The Qing then took the wealthy Yangtze delta, and Ming resistance retreated to the far south.

events.text: The last Southern Ming emperor, Yongli, is executed
events.detail: The Yongli Emperor, crowned in 1646, was the last and longest-lasting Southern Ming ruler, at times controlling much of southern China with the help of former rebel armies. Qing forces steadily pushed him west into Guizhou and Yunnan, and in 1659 he fled into Burma. In 1661 Wu Sangui, now a Qing general, invaded Burma, and the Burmese king handed Yongli over. He was executed in 1662. His death ended the Ming dynasty's claim on the mainland; only the Zheng regime on Taiwan still used the Ming name, until it surrendered to the Qing in 1683.

name: Portuguese Empire
summary: Portugal's seizure of Ceuta in 1415 opened a century of exploration down the African coast that reached India in 1498 and Brazil in 1500, and a chain of fortified ports from Goa to Malacca. The Dutch took much of its Asian trade in the 17th century, and Brazil became independent in 1822; Portugal then turned to Africa and held on to Angola and Mozambique through the colonial wars of 1961–1974, decolonising after the Carnation Revolution (Macau was handed over in 1999).

events.text: Portugal conquers Ceuta in North Africa
events.detail: In the early 15th century Portugal was a small kingdom whose rulers wanted gold, trade and crusading glory against the Muslim states of North Africa. Ceuta, a rich Marinid port facing Gibraltar across the strait, was a key end point of Saharan trade routes. On 21 August 1415 a fleet under King John I and his sons, including Prince Henry (later called the Navigator), landed and took the city in a carefully prepared attack. Ceuta became Portugal's first overseas possession and a base for further raids. Its conquest is often taken as the start of the Portuguese Empire and of European overseas expansion.

events.text: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
events.detail: Through the 15th century Portuguese captains sailed further down the coast of West Africa, seeking gold, slaves and a sea route around Africa to the spices of Asia. In 1487 King John II sent Bartolomeu Dias south with three ships. Storms carried him beyond the southern tip of Africa, and in February 1488 he reached Mossel Bay and sailed on to Kwaaihoek, near the Boesmans River, before his restless crew persuaded him to turn back. On the way home, in May 1488, he sighted the Cape of Good Hope. Dias had proved that the Atlantic and Indian oceans were connected, opening the sea route to India.

events.text: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut by sea
events.detail: King Manuel I sent Vasco da Gama with four ships to follow up Dias's discovery. Da Gama left Lisbon in July 1497, rounded the Cape, called at Mozambique, Mombasa and Malindi on the East African coast, and with the help of a local pilot crossed the Indian Ocean to reach Calicut, on India's Malabar Coast, in May 1498. Relations with the ruler, the Zamorin, were tense, but da Gama returned in 1499 with a cargo of spices that made the voyage highly profitable. It was the first direct sea voyage from Europe to India, and it made Portugal the first European power in the Indian Ocean trade.

events.text: Cabral reaches the coast of Brazil
events.detail: In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral led a second, much larger fleet of 13 ships to India. Sailing far out into the Atlantic to catch favourable winds, he made landfall in April 1500. The land lay in Portugal's half of the world under the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), so he claimed it, naming it the Island of the True Cross, before continuing to India. Whether the landfall was an accident or planned is still debated. Brazil grew into Portugal's largest and richest colony, first for brazilwood and sugar, later for gold, and gave the empire its huge territory in South America.

events.text: Afonso de Albuquerque conquers Goa
events.detail: To control the spice trade the Portuguese needed fortified bases in Asia, not just trading posts. Afonso de Albuquerque, governor of Portuguese India, took Goa from the Sultanate of Bijapur in early 1510, lost it within months, and retook it with a larger force on 25 November 1510. Goa, an island port on India's west coast, became the capital of the Estado da Índia, Portugal's network of forts and trading towns from East Africa to East Asia. It stayed Portuguese for more than 450 years, until India annexed it in 1961.

events.text: Malacca captured
events.detail: Malacca, on the strait between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, was the greatest trading port of Southeast Asia, where spices from the Moluccas and goods from China and India changed hands. After a Portuguese trading mission was attacked there, Albuquerque sailed from Goa with about 1,000 soldiers and some Indian allies. After weeks of fighting, the city fell in August 1511 and the sultan fled. The Portuguese built the fortress of A Famosa and controlled the strait for 130 years. Malacca gave Portugal a base for reaching the Spice Islands, China and Japan.

events.text: Philip II of Spain becomes king: the Iberian Union (to 1640)
events.detail: King Sebastian of Portugal was killed in Morocco at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, leaving no heir, and his elderly great-uncle, Cardinal Henry, died in 1580. Philip II of Spain, a grandson of King Manuel I, pressed his claim with an army that defeated his rival, António, Prior of Crato, and in 1581 the Cortes of Tomar accepted him as Philip I of Portugal. Portugal kept its own laws and administration, but shared a king with Spain for 60 years. During the Iberian Union, Spain's enemies, above all the Dutch, attacked Portuguese trading posts and colonies around the world.

events.text: Malacca falls to the Dutch
events.detail: After throwing off Spanish rule in 1640, Portugal was still at war with the Dutch, whose East India Company had been seizing its Asian trade. The Dutch, allied with the Sultanate of Johor, besieged Malacca from August 1640. After more than five months of blockade, starvation and disease, the Portuguese garrison surrendered on 14 January 1641. Malacca became a Dutch possession. The loss ended Portuguese control of the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea and marked the shift of Asian sea power from Portugal to the Netherlands.

events.text: Brazil declares independence
events.detail: When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1807, the royal family and court fled to Brazil, and Rio de Janeiro became the capital of the empire; in 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal to Portugal. After King John VI returned to Lisbon in 1821, the Portuguese parliament tried to reduce Brazil to colonial status again. His son Pedro, left behind as regent, refused, and on 7 September 1822 declared Brazil independent, becoming its emperor. After a short war, Portugal recognised independence in 1825. The empire lost its largest and richest territory, leaving only scattered colonies in Africa and Asia.

events.text: British Ultimatum blocks Portugal's plan to link Angola and Mozambique
events.detail: In the 'Scramble for Africa', Portugal hoped to join Angola and Mozambique with a broad band of territory across central Africa, the 'Pink Map'. This clashed with British interests pressed by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and by British missionaries north of the Zambezi. On 11 January 1890 Britain sent an ultimatum demanding that Portuguese forces withdraw from the lands between the two colonies, in what became Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi. Portugal gave way. The humiliation fed republican anger that helped bring down the monarchy in 1910, and Angola and Mozambique stayed separate.

events.text: Colonial war begins in Angola; India annexes Goa, Daman and Diu
events.detail: After the Second World War most European empires were giving up their colonies, but Portugal's dictatorship, the Estado Novo, insisted its colonies were overseas provinces of one nation. In February and March 1961 armed uprisings broke out in Angola, beginning the colonial wars that later spread to Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. In December 1961 India, after years of failed negotiations, sent its army into Goa, Daman and Diu and took them in about two days. Portugal lost its oldest colonies in Asia, and from 1961 it fought three wars in Africa for 13 years.

events.text: Carnation Revolution in Lisbon ends the colonial war
events.detail: By the early 1970s the colonial wars took a large share of Portugal's budget and kept many thousands of young men under arms, with no victory in sight. On 25 April 1974 junior officers of the Armed Forces Movement overthrew the Estado Novo dictatorship in an almost bloodless coup; crowds put carnations in the soldiers' rifles, giving the Carnation Revolution its name. The new government quickly agreed to end the wars and grant independence. Guinea-Bissau's independence was recognised in 1974, and Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe and Angola followed in 1975, ending Portugal's African empire.

events.text: Angola becomes independent on 11 November
events.detail: Angola was Portugal's largest and richest colony, but three rival independence movements fought there: the MPLA, the FNLA and UNITA. In January 1975 Portugal and the three signed the Alvor Agreement, setting 11 November 1975 as the date for independence under a shared transitional government, but the coalition soon collapsed into civil war, with foreign powers backing different sides. As the last Portuguese troops left, the MPLA, holding the capital Luanda, proclaimed the People's Republic of Angola on 11 November 1975. With Angola gone, almost nothing remained of the Portuguese Empire except Macau, returned to China in 1999.

name: Russian Empire (Muscovy, Tsardom and Empire)
summary: Ivan III gathered the Russian principalities under Moscow and threw off Tatar overlordship; Ivan IV took the title of tsar in 1547 and conquered the Volga khanates, opening the way for Cossacks and traders to cross Siberia to the Pacific within a century. Peter the Great's victory over Sweden made Russia an empire in 1721, and expansion into Poland, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Amur followed until it reached its greatest extent in the late 19th century, before defeat by Japan and the First World War brought revolution in 1917.

events.text: Ivan III annexes Novgorod
events.detail: In the 15th century Novgorod was a wealthy merchant republic ruling a vast territory stretching to the Arctic and the Urals, and Moscow's Grand Prince Ivan III wanted to bring all the Russian lands under his rule. When Novgorod's leaders turned towards Lithuania, Ivan defeated its army at the Shelon River in 1471. In 1478 he besieged the city again and forced its surrender; the republic's assembly was abolished and its famous bell taken to Moscow. Annexing Novgorod added its vast northern lands to Muscovy and made Moscow the dominant Russian state.

events.text: Great Stand on the Ugra River ends Tatar overlordship
events.detail: For two centuries the Russian principalities had paid tribute to the Golden Horde, the Mongol-Tatar state of the steppe. Ivan III stopped paying, and in 1480 Khan Akhmat of the Great Horde marched north to force him, hoping to join his Lithuanian allies. The two armies faced each other across the Ugra River, southwest of Moscow, for weeks in October and November, but the Tatars never managed to cross, Lithuanian help did not arrive, and winter set in. Akhmat withdrew without a battle. The 'Great Stand' is traditionally taken as the end of the Tatar yoke, leaving Moscow a fully sovereign state.

events.text: Ivan IV crowned the first Tsar of all Russia
events.detail: Ivan IV, grand prince of Moscow since the age of three, took power in his own right as a teenager. On 16 January 1547 he was crowned in Moscow's Dormition Cathedral as 'Tsar of all Russia', a title derived from the Latin 'caesar' and meant as the equal of 'emperor'. The new title claimed a status equal to the greatest monarchs and marked the start of the Tsardom of Russia. Ivan, later known as 'the Terrible', went on to reform the law and the army and to begin Russia's expansion to the east.

events.text: Kazan Khanate conquered (Astrakhan follows in 1556)
events.detail: The Khanate of Kazan, a successor state of the Golden Horde on the middle Volga, had fought Moscow on and off for more than a century. After failed campaigns, Ivan IV built a fortress at Sviyazhsk near Kazan and besieged the city in 1552 with a large army and siege engineers; on 2 October his troops blew up the walls with mines and stormed it. In 1556 Russian forces also took the Khanate of Astrakhan at the mouth of the Volga. Russia now controlled the whole Volga route to the Caspian Sea and opened the way to the Urals and Siberia.

events.text: c. 1582: Yermak's Cossacks defeat the Khanate of Sibir
events.detail: The merchant Stroganov family, who held vast lands in the Urals, hired a band of Cossacks under the ataman Yermak Timofeyevich to protect them against the Siberian Khanate of Kuchum Khan. In about 1581–82 Yermak led some 840 men across the Urals along the rivers; with firearms against bows, they defeated Kuchum's forces near the Irtysh and took his capital, Qashliq (Sibir). Yermak was killed in an ambush by Kuchum's men in 1584 or 1585 (sources differ), but Russian forts followed. The conquest opened Siberia, and by 1639 Russian explorers and fur traders had reached the Pacific Ocean.

events.text: Mikhail Romanov elected tsar, ending the Time of Troubles
events.detail: After the old Rurikid dynasty died out in 1598, Russia fell into the 'Time of Troubles': famine, civil war, pretenders claiming to be the dead Tsarevich Dmitry, and invasion by Poland-Lithuania and Sweden. Polish troops even occupied Moscow until a volunteer army raised by Kuzma Minin and led by Prince Dmitry Pozharsky drove them out in 1612. In February 1613 an Assembly of the Land (Zemsky Sobor) elected 16-year-old Mikhail Romanov as tsar. The Romanov dynasty would rule Russia for over 300 years, until 1917, though peace with Sweden and Poland cost land to both.

events.text: Treaty of Pereyaslav brings the Dnieper Cossacks under Moscow
events.detail: In 1648 the Zaporozhian Cossacks of Ukraine under Bohdan Khmelnytsky rose against Polish-Lithuanian rule and, needing a powerful ally, turned to the Orthodox tsar. In January 1654 a council of Cossack officers at Pereiaslav agreed to accept the authority of Tsar Alexis, which brought Russia into a long war with Poland-Lithuania. The exact meaning of the agreement, alliance or submission, is still disputed by Ukrainian and Russian historians. By the Truce of Andrusovo (1667) Russia gained Smolensk and the Ukrainian lands east of the Dnieper, plus the city of Kyiv, handed over at first for two years, a major shift of power in eastern Europe.

events.text: Treaty of Nerchinsk fixes the border with Qing China
events.detail: As Russian explorers and fur traders pushed into the Amur River valley in the mid-17th century, they clashed with the Qing dynasty, which ruled Manchuria and besieged the Russian fort at Albazin in 1685–86. In 1689 envoys of the two empires met at Nerchinsk, with Jesuit priests acting as interpreters in Latin, and signed China's first treaty with a European state. Russia gave up the Amur basin and the border was set along the Argun River and the Stanovoy Mountains, but it gained the right to trade with China. The border held for about 170 years.

events.text: Treaty of Nystad ends the Great Northern War; empire proclaimed
events.detail: Peter the Great wanted a 'window on the West' on the Baltic Sea, then dominated by Sweden. In the Great Northern War (1700–21) Russia, after an early disaster at Narva in 1700, crushed Charles XII's army at Poltava in 1709 and built a navy and the new capital of Saint Petersburg on conquered land. By the Treaty of Nystad, signed on 10 September 1721, Sweden ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and part of Karelia. Russia became the leading power of northern Europe, and in 1721 Peter became the first Emperor of Russia, turning the tsardom into the Russian Empire.

events.text: Catherine II annexes the Crimean Khanate
events.detail: The Crimean Khanate, long an Ottoman vassal that raided Russian and Ukrainian lands, had been declared independent by the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774, but it was really under Russian influence. After repeated unrest, Catherine the Great formally annexed the khanate by a manifesto on 19 April 1783 (8 April, Old Style), on the urging of her adviser Prince Grigory Potemkin. Work soon began on a port at Akhtiar, the future Sevastopol, as the base for a new Black Sea Fleet. Russia now had a firm hold on the northern coast of the Black Sea.

events.text: Final partition of Poland-Lithuania
events.detail: In the late 18th century the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, weakened by a paralysed political system, was partitioned three times by its neighbours Russia, Prussia and Austria. After the Kościuszko Uprising of 1794 was crushed by Russian and Prussian armies, the three powers agreed in 1795 to divide what remained, and Poland-Lithuania disappeared from the map for 123 years. In this third partition Russia took the rest of Lithuania. Over the three partitions Russia gained the largest share of the Commonwealth's people, and its border moved deep into central Europe.

events.text: Convention of Peking: land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri
events.detail: While Britain and France fought China in the Second Opium War, Russia pressed the Qing for the lands along the Amur River given up at Nerchinsk. By the Treaty of Aigun (1858) China ceded the left bank of the Amur, and after the Anglo-French capture of Beijing in 1860 the Russian envoy Nikolay Ignatyev obtained the Convention of Peking, which also gave Russia the land between the Ussuri River and the Pacific coast. Together the two treaties gave Russia roughly 1 million km² and a long Pacific coastline, where it founded Vladivostok, and cut China off from the Sea of Japan.

events.text: Alaska sold to the United States
events.detail: Russian Alaska was valued mainly for sea-otter furs, but by the 1850s the otters had been hunted almost to extinction, few Russians lived there, and Russia, short of money after its defeat in the Crimean War, could not easily defend it. On 30 March 1867 the United States agreed to buy Alaska for 7.2 million US dollars, about 2 cents an acre; the transfer took effect on 18 October 1867. Russia gave up its only lands in the Americas. Its eastward expansion now ended at the Bering Strait.

events.text: Defeat by Japan; Treaty of Portsmouth cedes southern Sakhalin
events.detail: Russia and Japan both wanted control of Manchuria and Korea, and Russia had leased Port Arthur in China as a naval base. In February 1904 Japan attacked the Russian fleet there, then besieged and took the port and won the land battle of Mukden; in May 1905 it destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima. US President Theodore Roosevelt mediated peace, and on 5 September 1905 the Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan the lease of the Liaodong Peninsula, Russia's railway in southern Manchuria and the southern half of Sakhalin. The defeat helped spark the Revolution of 1905 and checked Russian expansion in East Asia.

events.text: February Revolution: Nicholas II abdicates; republic proclaimed
events.detail: Three years of the First World War brought Russia huge losses, food shortages and anger at Tsar Nicholas II's government. In late February 1917 (March, New Style) strikes and bread riots in Petrograd turned into revolution when soldiers of the garrison joined the crowds. On 2 March (15 March) Nicholas abdicated, ending more than 300 years of Romanov rule. A Provisional Government took power alongside the workers' and soldiers' soviets, and in September proclaimed Russia a republic. The empire's collapse let Finland, Poland and other borderlands break away, before the Bolsheviks seized power in October.

reigns.name: Peter I the Great (with Ivan V to 1696)

name: Spanish Empire

chain.clio: (Personal union of Crown of Aragon with Crown of Castile)

summary: Castile and Aragon completed the conquest of Granada and sponsored Columbus in 1492; within two generations Spain had overthrown the Aztec and Inca states and spread from the Americas to the Philippines, and from 1580 to 1640 its king also ruled Portugal. The empire reached its greatest extent in the late 18th century, lost the American mainland in the wars of independence (1808–1826), and lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines in 1898; its last African territories were given up in 1956–1976.

events.text: Granada conquered; Columbus reaches the Caribbean
events.detail: The marriage of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon had joined Spain's two largest kingdoms, and from 1482 they waged a ten-year war against Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia. On 2 January 1492 its last sultan, Boabdil, surrendered the city, completing the Christian 'Reconquista'. That spring the monarchs agreed to sponsor Christopher Columbus, who sailed west hoping to reach Asia and on 12 October 1492 landed in the Bahamas, then reached Cuba and Hispaniola. In one year Spain was united under Christian rule and gained the first foothold of an empire in the Americas.

events.text: Fall of Tenochtitlan: Spanish rule in Mexico begins
events.detail: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with a few hundred Spaniards and marched inland, gaining tens of thousands of allies among peoples who resented Aztec rule, above all the Tlaxcalans. Driven out of the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1520, he returned with his allies and boats built for the lake and besieged the island city from late May, while smallpox devastated its people. On 13 August 1521 the last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, was captured and the city fell. Spain built Mexico City on its ruins, and New Spain became the core of its empire in North America.

events.text: Pizarro captures Atahualpa at Cajamarca; conquest of the Inca begins
events.detail: The Inca Empire, the largest state in the Americas, had just been torn apart by a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar, and weakened by epidemics. Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than 200 Spaniards, met the victorious Atahualpa at Cajamarca in the Andes on 16 November 1532. In a surprise attack using guns, horses and steel, the Spaniards killed many of the emperor's unarmed attendants and took him prisoner. Atahualpa paid a huge ransom in gold and silver but was executed in 1533. Spain went on to take Cusco and the Inca lands, and Peru became a second great centre of its American empire.

events.text: Legazpi arrives in the Philippines: the Spanish East Indies begin
events.detail: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition had reached the Philippines for Spain in 1521, but no lasting colony followed. In 1564 Miguel López de Legazpi sailed from New Spain (Mexico) with about 500 men, and in 1565 he founded the first Spanish settlement at Cebu. In the same year his navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found a route back across the Pacific to Mexico, which made regular trade possible. Legazpi founded Manila in 1571 and made it the capital. The Philippines became Spain's base in Asia for over 300 years, linked to Mexico by the Manila galleons carrying American silver to China.

events.text: Philip II takes the Portuguese throne: the Iberian Union
events.detail: In 1578 the young King Sebastian of Portugal died in battle in Morocco without an heir, and his successor, Cardinal Henry, died in 1580. Philip II of Spain, a grandson of King Manuel I, claimed the throne and sent an army under the Duke of Alba, which defeated the rival claimant, António, Prior of Crato, near Lisbon. In 1581 the Cortes of Tomar accepted Philip as king. Portugal kept its own laws, but the union under one king joined the Spanish and Portuguese empires. Philip ruled the largest collection of territories in the world, from the Americas to Africa and Asia.

events.text: Portugal breaks away, ending the Iberian Union
events.detail: Under Philip IV, Spain's chief minister, the Count-Duke of Olivares, pressed Portugal to pay more and send troops for Spain's wars, while the Dutch seized Portuguese colonies. In 1640, as Spain was also fighting a revolt in Catalonia, Portuguese nobles rose in Lisbon on 1 December and proclaimed the Duke of Braganza king as John IV. The Restoration War that followed lasted until 1668, when Spain recognised Portugal's independence in the Treaty of Lisbon. Spain lost Portugal and its empire in Brazil, Africa and Asia, though it kept Ceuta.

events.text: Treaties of Utrecht: Philip V keeps Spain; Gibraltar and Menorca go to Britain
events.detail: When the childless Charles II of Spain died in 1700, he left his throne to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France. Fearing a union of Spain and France, Britain, the Dutch Republic and Austria went to war. The Peace of Utrecht in 1713 let Philip V keep Spain and its American empire, on condition that he gave up any claim to the French throne. Under the Utrecht treaties and the related Treaty of Rastatt, Spain's lands in Italy and the southern Netherlands went mostly to Austria, with Sicily to Savoy, and Gibraltar and Menorca were ceded to Britain. Spain lost its European possessions outside Iberia but kept its empire overseas.

events.text: Napoleon invades; the wars of independence in America begin
events.detail: In 1808 Napoleon forced Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII to give up the Spanish crown and made his own brother Joseph king. Spaniards rose against the French on 2 May 1808 in Madrid, beginning the long Peninsular War, in which British troops fought alongside Spanish and Portuguese forces. With the king a prisoner in France, local juntas in the American colonies took over government in his name, and from 1810 many moved towards independence. The crisis broke Spain's hold on its American empire and began the wars of independence that ended it on the mainland by the mid-1820s.

events.text: Royalist defeat at Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in South America
events.detail: After 1810 independence movements led by Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and others gradually freed most of Spanish South America, but royalist armies still held the highlands of Peru. On 9 December 1824 a patriot army under Simón Bolívar's lieutenant Antonio José de Sucre defeated a royalist army of similar or larger size near Ayacucho in Peru. The wounded viceroy, José de la Serna, was captured, and the royal army of Peru capitulated. The battle effectively ended Spanish rule in South America; the last royalist strongholds, at Callao and Chiloé, held out until 1826, leaving only Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Americas.

events.text: Spanish–American War: Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam lost
events.detail: In 1895 Cubans rose again against Spanish rule, and the harsh Spanish response angered the United States. After the US battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour in February 1898, the United States declared war in April. The US Navy destroyed Spanish fleets at Manila Bay and off Santiago de Cuba, and US troops landed in Cuba and Puerto Rico. By the Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 December 1898, Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States. Spain's empire, once worldwide, was reduced to a few territories in Africa.

events.text: Spanish protectorate in northern Morocco established
events.detail: European powers were dividing North Africa, and France and Spain had agreed to share influence in Morocco. After France imposed a protectorate on the Sultan of Morocco in the Treaty of Fez in March 1912, a Franco-Spanish treaty in November 1912 gave Spain a protectorate over a strip of northern Morocco, including the Rif mountains, with its capital at Tetuán. Spain faced fierce resistance there, notably the Rif War of the 1920s led by Abd el-Krim. The protectorate was Spain's main new colony in the 20th century, and it was where Francisco Franco's army rose in revolt in 1936.

events.text: Northern Morocco joins independent Morocco
events.detail: After the Second World War, nationalist movements across North Africa demanded independence. France ended its protectorate in Morocco in March 1956, and Spain, under Franco, soon followed. On 7 April 1956 Spain recognised Morocco's independence and gave up its protectorate in the north, keeping the cities of Ceuta and Melilla. After the short Ifni War, Spain ceded the southern zone around Cape Juby in 1958, and it kept the enclave of Sidi Ifni until 1969. Spain's remaining African empire was now mainly the Spanish Sahara.

events.text: Madrid Accords: Spain agrees to leave Western Sahara (withdrawal 1976)
events.detail: Spanish Sahara, a desert colony on the Atlantic coast, was claimed by both Morocco and Mauritania, while the Polisario Front fought for independence. On 6 November 1975, with Franco dying, King Hassan II of Morocco sent some 350,000 unarmed marchers across the border in the 'Green March'. On 14 November Spain signed the Madrid Accords, agreeing to hand over administration to Morocco and Mauritania. Spain withdrew in early 1976, and Morocco and Mauritania moved in. The withdrawal ended Spain's colonial empire in Africa, though the status of Western Sahara remains disputed.

reigns.name: Isabella I and Ferdinand II, the Catholic Monarchs (r. from 1474/1479)

name: Safavid Empire
summary: Ismail I, head of the Safavid Sufi order, was enthroned at Tabriz in 1501 and within a decade had conquered Iran and Iraq and imposed Twelver Shi'ism. Defeat at Chaldiran in 1514 fixed a long frontier war with the Ottomans; Abbas I (1587–1629) rebuilt the state from Isfahan and won back lost ground, but Afghan invaders took Isfahan in 1722 and Nader Shah ended the dynasty in 1736.

events.text: Ismail I takes Baghdad, ending the Aq Qoyunlu
events.detail: Ismail, the young leader of the Safavid Sufi order backed by the Turkmen Qizilbash tribes, had seized Tabriz in 1501 and proclaimed himself shah, making Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran. He then spent several years overthrowing the Aq Qoyunlu, the Turkmen dynasty that had ruled western Iran and Iraq. In 1508 Ismail and his commander Husayn Beg Shamlu took Baghdad, putting an end to the Aq Qoyunlu, and began destroying Sunni shrines there. With Mesopotamia added, the Safavids now ruled from the Caucasus to the Persian Gulf, though Baghdad would change hands several times in later wars with the Ottomans.

events.text: Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani defeated and killed near Merv
events.detail: To the northeast, the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani Khan had conquered Transoxiana and the Timurid lands of Khorasan, and raided into Iran. In 1510 Shah Ismail marched east with great speed; Shaybani, short of troops, retreated behind the walls of Merv (in today's Turkmenistan). On 2 December 1510 the Safavid army feigned a retreat, drew the Uzbeks out of the fortress and ambushed them, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape. The victory gave the Safavids the rich province of Khorasan, including Herat, and pushed the frontier with the Uzbeks back towards the Oxus (Amu Darya), although the Uzbeks went on raiding Khorasan for a century.

events.text: Ottoman victory at Chaldiran; eastern Anatolia lost
events.detail: Ismail's preaching among the Turkmen tribes of eastern Anatolia alarmed the Sunni Ottoman Sultan Selim I, who marched east in 1514. On 23 August the two armies met at Chaldiran, northwest of Lake Urmia. The Ottomans, with an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 men, heavy artillery and musket-armed Janissaries, crushed the Safavid cavalry, which had no artillery; Ismail was wounded and nearly captured. Selim briefly occupied the Safavid capital, Tabriz. The Ottomans annexed eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia, ending Safavid expansion to the west, and Ismail never again led an army in battle.

events.text: Peace of Amasya with the Ottomans after decades of war
events.detail: Under Ismail's son Tahmasp I, the Safavids fought a long war with Suleiman the Magnificent, who invaded Iran and took Baghdad in the mid-1530s. On 29 May 1555 the two empires signed the Peace of Amasya, the first formal peace between them. Armenia and Georgia were divided, with the western parts going to the Ottomans and the eastern parts staying with Iran, and the Ottomans kept most of Iraq, including Baghdad. The treaty set a frontier that brought about twenty years of peace.

events.text: Abbas I makes Isfahan the capital
events.detail: Abbas I became shah in 1587 at a low point: the Ottomans held Tabriz and much of the northwest, and the Uzbeks had overrun half of Khorasan. After making peace with the Ottomans in 1590 and rebuilding his army, he decided to move the capital to a safer, more central place. In 1598 he moved it from Qazvin to Isfahan and rebuilt the city as one of the largest of the 17th century, around the vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square, with new mosques, palaces, bazaars and bridges. Isfahan became the political and cultural heart of Safavid Iran, and the saying went that 'Isfahan is half the world'.

events.text: Abbas I retakes Tabriz from the Ottomans
events.detail: In the peace of 1590 Abbas had been forced to give the Ottomans large territories, including Tabriz, the old Safavid capital. With a reformed army that included musketeers, artillery and ghulams (slave soldiers recruited mainly from the Caucasus), he opened a new war in 1603. His troops retook Tabriz in 1603, then Erivan, Shirvan and other lands. By 1612 the Safavids had regained all the territory ceded in 1590, including Azerbaijan, Georgia and Shirvan. It was the first great Safavid victory over the Ottomans and restored the empire's northwest.

events.text: Hormuz taken from the Portuguese with English help; Kandahar seized
events.detail: Since 1507 the Portuguese had held a fortress on the island of Hormuz, controlling the Persian Gulf trade between India and Europe. In 1622 Abbas I's general Imam Quli Khan besieged it, with ships of the English East India Company, which wanted Persian trade, providing naval support; after a siege from February to April the Portuguese surrendered. In the same year, from May, Safavid forces besieged and captured the fortress city of Kandahar from the Mughal emperor Jahangir. Both gains extended Safavid power: the empire controlled the gulf coast, while Kandahar became its eastern bastion against India.

events.text: Abbas I recaptures Baghdad (1623–24)
events.detail: In a new war with Sultan Murad IV, which Abbas I presented as a defence of Shiism, a Safavid army besieged Baghdad, held by the Ottoman officer Bakr Subashi. It broke into the city on 12 January 1624 and had taken it two days later, and many Sunni inhabitants were massacred. Fighting spread to other cities of Ottoman Iraq, including Mosul, Kirkuk and Basra. Mesopotamia, with its Shia shrine cities such as Najaf and Karbala, was back in Safavid hands for the first time since the 1530s. The Ottomans repeatedly tried to recover Baghdad and finally retook it in 1638 under Sultan Murad IV.

events.text: Treaty of Zuhab: Baghdad and Mesopotamia ceded to the Ottomans
events.detail: After Abbas I died in 1629 the Safavids faced renewed Ottoman offensives, and in 1638 Sultan Murad IV recaptured Baghdad. On 17 May 1639 the two empires made peace at Qasr-e Shirin, in western Iran, in the Treaty of Zuhab. It largely confirmed the Peace of Amasya: the Caucasus was permanently divided, with eastern Armenia, eastern Georgia, Dagestan and Shirvan staying Safavid, and Iran gave up all of Mesopotamia, including Baghdad. The treaty ended almost 150 years of intermittent war, and its line became the rough outline of today's frontier between Iran and Turkey and Iraq.

events.text: Afghan Hotaki army takes Isfahan; Soltan Hoseyn deposed
events.detail: By the early 18th century the Safavid state was weak, with poor leadership and court intrigue. Afghan Ghilzai tribes in Kandahar, led by the Hotaki family, rebelled, and in 1722 Mahmud Hotak marched deep into Iran. On 8 March 1722 his much smaller army routed the Safavid army at Gulnabad, near Isfahan, and then besieged the capital. After months of famine, Shah Soltan Hoseyn capitulated on 23 October 1722 and abdicated in favour of Mahmud. The Afghans would hold much of Iran until 1729, while the Ottomans and Russians seized lands in the west and north.

events.text: Nader recovers Iran for Tahmasp II after the Afghan occupation
events.detail: After Isfahan fell, the shah's son Tahmasp escaped and claimed the throne as Tahmasp II, but he had little power. Nader, an Afshar Turkmen warlord from Khorasan and a brilliant general, became the commander of his army and recaptured Mashhad in late 1726. In September 1729 Nader defeated the Afghan ruler Ashraf at Damghan, then decisively in November at Murchakhort, and in December he handed Isfahan back to Tahmasp. The Safavids were restored in name, but real power lay with Nader, who went on to drive the Ottomans and Russians out of the lands they had taken.

events.text: Nader Shah crowned; the Safavid dynasty ends
events.detail: Nader steadily took control of the state: in 1732 he forced Tahmasp II to abdicate in favour of his infant son, Abbas III, and ruled as regent while winning wars against the Ottomans. In 1736, after recovering the empire's lost territories, he deposed the child and was crowned shah himself on 8 March 1736, founding the Afsharid dynasty. The Safavids, who had ruled Iran since 1501, lost the throne for good. Under Nader the empire briefly expanded again, invading Mughal India and sacking Delhi in 1739.

name: Mughal Empire
summary: Babur, a Timurid prince from Kabul, defeated the Delhi sultan at Panipat in 1526; his son Humayun lost the realm to Sher Shah Suri and won it back in 1555. Akbar and his successors built one of the largest states in Indian history, which reached its widest extent under Aurangzeb (d. 1707) after the conquest of the Deccan sultanates. It then fragmented under Maratha, Persian, Afghan and British pressure, and the British deposed the last emperor after the 1857 rebellion.

events.text: Sher Shah Suri drives Humayun out of India
events.detail: Babur had founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, but his son Humayun faced a powerful rival in Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan commander who had built up power in Bihar and Bengal. Sher Shah crushed Humayun's army at Chausa on 26 June 1539, and Humayun barely escaped by swimming the Ganges. On 17 May 1540 the two met again at Kannauj (Bilgram), and the Mughals were routed. Humayun fled through Lahore and Sindh and eventually took refuge at the court of the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I in Persia. Sher Shah founded the Sur Empire, ruling from Delhi, and Mughal rule in India collapsed for 15 years.

events.text: Humayun returns from Persia and retakes Delhi
events.detail: After Sher Shah's son Islam Shah died in 1554, the Sur Empire broke apart among quarrelling rivals. Humayun, who had spent years in exile in Persia and had won back Kandahar and Kabul with Safavid help, saw his chance and invaded the Punjab with his general Bairam Khan. On 22 June 1555 his army decisively defeated Sikandar Shah Suri at Sirhind, and on 23 July 1555 Humayun sat once again on the throne in Delhi. The Mughal Empire was restored, though Humayun died only six months later, in January 1556, leaving his 13-year-old son Akbar to rebuild it.

events.text: Akbar's army wins the Second Battle of Panipat
events.detail: Soon after Humayun's death, Hemu (Hemchandra), a Hindu general of the Sur dynasty, defeated the Mughals at Delhi, took Delhi and Agra, and crowned himself king as Vikramaditya. Akbar, aged 13, and his guardian Bairam Khan marched to take them back. On 5 November 1556 the armies met at Panipat, near the site of Babur's victory 30 years earlier. Hemu seemed close to winning when an arrow struck him in the eye; he fell unconscious, his army fled, and he was captured and beheaded. The victory recovered Delhi and Agra and secured Akbar's throne, starting nearly 50 years of Mughal expansion.

events.text: Malwa annexed
events.detail: Malwa, a rich plateau in central India, was ruled by Baz Bahadur, son of a former Sur governor, who had declared himself independent in 1555. Malwa controlled key routes between northern India, Gujarat and the Deccan. In 1561 Akbar sent an army under Adham Khan and Pir Muhammad Khan, which defeated Baz Bahadur at the Battle of Sarangpur on 29 March 1561. Baz Bahadur fled, and Mughal rule over Malwa was completed by 1562, when it became a Mughal province (subah). The conquest carried the empire's frontier south into central India, towards Gujarat and the Deccan sultanates.

events.text: Chittorgarh falls after a long siege
events.detail: The Sisodia rulers of Mewar were the leading Rajput dynasty still refusing to accept Mughal overlordship, and their fortress of Chittorgarh, on a high rocky plateau, was one of the strongest in India. Akbar besieged it with a large army and artillery from 23 October 1567, while Rana Udai Singh withdrew to the hills and left the fort under Jaimal Rathore. After four months of mining and assaults, Jaimal was killed by a musket shot on 22 February 1568, and the fort fell the next day; many defenders and thousands of non-combatants were killed. The fall of Chittor led most other Rajput states to accept Mughal rule.

events.text: Conquest of Gujarat completed
events.detail: Gujarat, on India's west coast, had rich farmland, a large textile industry and the busiest seaports in India, and it sheltered rebels against Akbar. In 1572 Akbar occupied Ahmedabad, the capital, and was proclaimed ruler of Gujarat, and by 1573 he had driven out the rebel Mirzas. The last sultan, Muzaffar Shah III, was taken prisoner to Agra, and Gujarat became a Mughal province in 1573. The conquest gave the empire its first outlet to the Arabian Sea, with ports such as Surat, and a link to the trade of Asia, Africa and Europe.

events.text: Victory at Rajmahal secures Bengal
events.detail: Bengal, the rich delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra, was ruled by the Afghan Karrani dynasty, whose last sultan, Daud Khan, had defied Akbar. Mughal armies under Khan Jahan and Todar Mal defeated Daud's forces at Rajmahal, on the Ganges at the gateway to Bengal, on 12 July 1576. Daud was captured and executed, and the Bengal Sultanate came to an end. Bengal became a Mughal province (subah), although Afghan and local chiefs went on resisting for years. Its wealth made it one of the empire's most valuable provinces, and it extended Mughal rule east to the Bay of Bengal.

events.text: Kabul formally annexed
events.detail: Kabul, the old base of Babur and Humayun, had been ruled almost independently by Akbar's half-brother, Mirza Muhammad Hakim, who more than once tried to seize the Mughal throne. In the early 1580s Akbar's forces occupied Kabul and forced his brother into submission. When Muhammad Hakim died on 10 October 1585, Akbar took direct control, and Kabul was formally made a province of the empire. Akbar then moved his court to Lahore and spent the next thirteen years in the northwest. The annexation secured the empire's frontier in Afghanistan and its routes to Central Asia, and pushed its border towards the Hindu Kush.

events.text: Asirgarh taken after Ahmadnagar (1600): Mughals enter the Deccan
events.detail: With northern India secured, Akbar turned south against the Deccan sultanates, which had refused to submit. After earlier campaigns, his forces took the fortress of Ahmadnagar in August 1600, defended earlier by Chand Bibi. Akbar then besieged Asirgarh, a hill fortress called the 'key to the Deccan', held by Miran Bahadur Shah of Khandesh, and took it on 17 January 1601, by some accounts through trickery rather than assault. Akbar created the provinces of Ahmadnagar, Berar and Khandesh. The Mughals now had a firm foothold in the Deccan, beginning a southward push that lasted a century.

events.text: Aurangzeb besieges and takes Golconda; Deccan sultanates absorbed
events.detail: Aurangzeb, emperor from 1658, spent the last decades of his reign in the Deccan, fighting the Marathas and the sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda. After conquering Bijapur in 1686, he personally besieged Golconda, the great fortress of the Qutb Shahi kings, from 28 January 1687. The siege dragged on for about eight months amid famine, monsoon floods and epidemic, until a defector let Mughal troops in by a back entrance and the main gate was opened on 22 September. The last king, Abul Hasan Qutb Shah, was imprisoned. Golconda became the province of Hyderabad, bringing almost all of southern India under Mughal rule.

events.text: Aurangzeb dies; the empire is at its greatest extent
events.detail: Aurangzeb died on 3 March 1707, aged 88, at Bhingar in the Deccan, where he had spent his last years campaigning. Under his rule the Mughal Empire had reached its greatest extent, spanning nearly the entire Indian subcontinent. But the long wars against the Marathas had drained the treasury, and his strict policies had alienated many Hindu, Sikh and Rajput subjects. His sons fought a war of succession, and the emperors who followed were weak. Within a few decades governors in Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad became independent in all but name, and the Marathas took over large parts of the empire.

events.text: Nader Shah of Persia sacks Delhi
events.detail: Nader Shah, the new ruler of Iran, invaded northern India in 1738, crossing the Indus at Attock. On 24 February 1739 his army routed the Mughals at Karnal, north of Delhi, and Emperor Muhammad Shah surrendered. The two entered Delhi together, but after riots on the night of 21 March in which some 3,000 Persian soldiers were killed, Nader ordered a massacre, and the city was sacked for several days. He carried off the Mughal treasury, the jewelled Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, and annexed all Mughal lands west of the Indus. The raid exposed the empire's weakness and stripped it of much of its wealth.

events.text: British East India Company wins at Plassey and takes control of Bengal
events.detail: In 1756 Siraj ud-Daulah, the young Nawab of Bengal, a governor who was now in practice independent of the Mughal emperor, captured the British East India Company's base at Calcutta. A Company force under Robert Clive retook it and then plotted with Siraj's commander, Mir Jafar, and wealthy bankers. On 23 June 1757, at Plassey, Clive's army of about 3,000 faced a Bengal army of around 50,000, but Mir Jafar's troops held back, and Siraj's army broke. Mir Jafar became nawab as a British puppet. Bengal, the richest Mughal province, came under the Company's control, the start of British rule in India.

events.text: Indian Rebellion; Bahadur Shah II deposed after the siege of Delhi
events.detail: On 10 May 1857 Indian soldiers (sepoys) of the East India Company mutinied at Meerut and marched to Delhi, where they proclaimed the 81-year-old Mughal ruler, Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), Emperor of Hindustan. The revolt spread across northern and central India. After a siege lasting from June to September 1857, British forces stormed Delhi; Bahadur Shah was captured at Humayun's Tomb on 20 September and later exiled to Rangoon in Burma, where he died in 1862. The Mughal dynasty, which had ruled since 1526, came to an end, and in 1858 the British Crown took over direct rule of India.

name: Dutch Colonial Empire
summary: The newly independent Dutch Republic built a commercial empire through the East India Company (VOC, 1602) and West India Company (1621), seizing Portuguese posts from Malacca to Ceylon and founding Batavia, New Amsterdam and the Cape Colony; it was at its height around 1652. Wars with England and France eroded it, but in the 19th century the Netherlands turned its foothold in the East Indies into a vast colony, lost to Japanese occupation in 1942 and to Indonesian independence in 1945–1949.

events.text: Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded
events.detail: In the 1590s, while still fighting for independence from Spain, Dutch merchants began sending fleets to the East Indies for pepper and spices, and several rival companies competed for the trade. To end the competition and take on Portugal and England, the States General merged them on 20 March 1602 into the United East India Company (VOC), with a 21-year monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia. It was one of the world's first joint-stock companies, whose shares any Dutch citizen could buy and trade. The VOC could build forts, keep armies and make treaties, and it became the main engine of the Dutch empire in Asia.

events.text: Coen takes Jakarta and refounds it as Batavia
events.detail: The VOC needed a permanent base in Asia to control the spice trade. In 1619 Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen captured the Javanese port of Jayakarta and built a new fortified town on its ruins, which the company named Batavia. Batavia, on the north coast of Java, became the centre of the VOC's trading network across Asia for nearly two centuries. Coen was ruthless: in 1621 he led the conquest of the Banda Islands, killing or enslaving much of the population to secure a monopoly on nutmeg. Batavia, today's Jakarta, remained the capital of the Dutch East Indies until 1942.

events.text: New Amsterdam founded in New Netherland
events.detail: The Dutch also traded in North America, where the Dutch West India Company founded the colony of New Netherland to run the fur trade along the Hudson River. In 1624–25 it built Fort Amsterdam at the southern tip of Manhattan; the settlement around it, New Amsterdam, became the colony's capital in 1625. It grew slowly, to about 2,500 people by 1664. That year the English seized it and renamed it New York, and after the Second Anglo-Dutch War the Dutch kept Suriname instead, ending their mainland colony in North America.

events.text: West India Company occupies Pernambuco: Dutch Brazil (to 1654)
events.detail: The Dutch West India Company, founded in 1621, aimed to attack the Atlantic empire of Spain and Portugal, then united under one king. In February 1630 its forces captured Olinda and Recife in Pernambuco, the heart of Brazil's sugar industry. Under Governor John Maurice of Nassau (1637–43) Dutch Brazil, with its capital at Recife, controlled almost half of Brazil's settled area, and artists and scientists recorded the land. But Portuguese settlers rose against Dutch rule and won battles at Guararapes in 1648 and 1649, and the Dutch surrendered Recife on 28 January 1654. In 1661 the Netherlands formally gave up Brazil.

events.text: Malacca taken from the Portuguese
events.detail: After Portugal broke away from Spain in 1640, it remained at war with the Dutch in Asia. The VOC, allied with the Sultanate of Johor, besieged Portuguese Malacca from August 1640. After more than five months of blockade, starvation and disease, the garrison surrendered on 14 January 1641. Malacca, which controlled the strait linking the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, became a Dutch possession for over 150 years. Its fall broke Portuguese power in the region and left the VOC the leading European power in the East Indies.

events.text: Cape Colony founded; the Dutch empire at its height
events.detail: VOC ships sailing between Europe and Asia needed a place to take on fresh water, meat and vegetables on the long voyage. In 1652 a VOC expedition led by Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay and built a fort, founding a supply station at the Cape of Good Hope. Much to the dismay of the company's shareholders, the Cape soon grew into a settler colony as farmers moved inland. By the mid-17th century the Dutch held trading posts and colonies from the Americas and Africa to India, Ceylon and the East Indies, the height of their overseas empire.

events.text: Conquest of Portuguese Ceylon completed
events.detail: The coasts of Ceylon (Sri Lanka), with their valuable trade, were held by the Portuguese. The king of Kandy, in the interior, invited the Dutch to help drive them out. The VOC took Negombo and Galle in 1640, and after a long war captured Colombo in 1656; by 1658 it had taken the last Portuguese strongholds. Colombo became the capital of Dutch Ceylon. The Dutch controlled most of the island's coasts but never conquered the Kingdom of Kandy, and Dutch Ceylon came to an end in 1796 when the British took over.

events.text: French-backed Batavian Republic; Britain occupies the Cape
events.detail: In January 1795 French revolutionary armies overran the Dutch Republic, and Dutch revolutionaries, with French support, proclaimed the Batavian Republic on 19 January, ending the rule of the stadtholder, William V. As the Netherlands was now a French ally, Britain began seizing Dutch colonies, and in 1795 British forces occupied the Cape of Good Hope. Other Dutch posts in Asia soon followed. The VOC, already in deep debt, was nationalised and dissolved at the end of 1799. The Dutch empire overseas was falling into British hands.

events.text: Kingdom of Holland annexed to Napoleon's French Empire (to 1813)
events.detail: In 1806 Napoleon turned the Batavian Republic into the Kingdom of Holland and made his brother Louis Bonaparte king. Louis tried to protect Dutch interests and did not strictly enforce Napoleon's Continental System against British trade, so smuggling continued. Losing patience, Napoleon sent troops, who took Amsterdam in early July 1810; Louis abdicated on 1 July, and on 9 July 1810 the kingdom was annexed to the French Empire. The Netherlands ceased to exist as a separate state until 1813, and with no Dutch government to defend them, the remaining Dutch colonies were exposed to British attack.

events.text: Anglo-Dutch Treaty returns the East Indies; the Cape stays British
events.detail: After Napoleon's defeat, Britain wanted a strong Netherlands as a buffer against France. By the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814, signed in London on 13 August, Britain returned most of the Dutch colonies it had occupied, including the Dutch East Indies, Malacca, Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean islands. In return the Dutch ceded the Cape Colony and parts of Guiana (later British Guiana) to Britain. The treaty restored the East Indies, the heart of the Dutch empire, but the Cape stayed British, ending Dutch rule in southern Africa.

events.text: Aceh War begins in northern Sumatra (to 1904)
events.detail: Aceh, a strong independent sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra, controlled the approaches to the Strait of Malacca and traded with other powers. In 1873 the Dutch declared war; the first expedition, sent in March, failed after its commander, General Köhler, was killed, and a second, larger force followed. Acehnese resistance, led by sultans, nobles such as Teuku Umar and Cut Nyak Dhien, and Islamic scholars, turned into a long guerrilla war. Some 37,000 soldiers on the Dutch side and 60,000–70,000 Acehnese died, many from cholera. By 1904 Aceh was conquered, completing Dutch rule over almost all of today's Indonesia.

events.text: Japan conquers the Dutch East Indies; Dutch surrender in March
events.detail: The Dutch East Indies were one of the world's leading oil exporters, which made them a prime target for Japan once war began with the Western powers in December 1941. Japanese forces invaded from January 1942, and destroyed much of the Allied fleet; the Dutch Admiral Karel Doorman was killed in the Battle of the Java Sea. Japanese troops landed on Java, and the campaign ended with the Allied surrender on 9 March 1942, with more than 100,000 Allied soldiers captured. The Japanese occupation of more than three years ended Dutch rule in practice and fuelled the movement for Indonesian independence.

events.text: Sovereignty transferred to Indonesia (independence proclaimed 1945)
events.detail: Two days after Japan surrendered, on 17 August 1945, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed Indonesia's independence. The Netherlands tried to restore its rule by force, but after a Dutch military offensive in 1948–49 the UN Security Council demanded that it stop and restore the republican government. At a Round Table Conference in The Hague, held from August to November 1949, the Dutch agreed to hand over sovereignty, and on 27 December 1949 power passed to the United States of Indonesia. The Netherlands lost its largest and richest colony, keeping only western New Guinea in Asia.

events.text: Dutch New Guinea handed to UN administration
events.detail: The Netherlands had kept western New Guinea in 1949, but Indonesia claimed it and threatened to take it by force. With the United States hosting talks, the two sides signed the New York Agreement at the United Nations on 15 August 1962. The territory was handed to a temporary UN administration, which handed it to Indonesia on 1 May 1963, with a promise of an 'act of free choice' by the inhabitants before 1969. The transfer ended Dutch rule in Asia after more than three and a half centuries, leaving only Suriname and the Caribbean islands.

events.text: Suriname becomes independent
events.detail: Suriname, on the northern coast of South America, had been a Dutch colony since 1667, when the Dutch kept it in exchange for New Amsterdam, and its plantations were worked by enslaved Africans until 1863. In 1954 it became an autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. A left-wing Dutch government took the initiative for full independence, which was granted after negotiations on 25 November 1975, followed by years of Dutch aid. With Suriname gone, only the small Caribbean islands remained of the Dutch empire.
