name: British Empire
summary: England's East India Company (1600) and its first American colonies grew into a worldwide empire of trading posts, settler colonies and conquests; the loss of the Thirteen Colonies in 1783 was offset by India, Australia, the Cape and footholds across Asia. Victory in the First World War added League of Nations mandates and the empire reached its largest extent around 1921, but the Dominions became self-governing, India won independence in 1947, and most remaining colonies followed by the 1960s; the handover of Hong Kong in 1997 is often taken as its end.

events.text: England takes Jamaica from Spain
events.detail: Oliver Cromwell, ruling England after the civil wars, planned a 'Western Design' to break Spanish power in the Caribbean and win new colonies. In April 1655 an English fleet under William Penn landed thousands of soldiers under Robert Venables near Santo Domingo on Hispaniola, but the attack failed with heavy losses. To salvage the expedition, they attacked poorly defended Spanish Jamaica and captured it in May 1655, though escaped slaves known as Maroons kept up resistance in the interior. Spain formally ceded the island in 1670. Jamaica became one of England's most valuable Caribbean colonies, and remained British until independence in 1962.

events.text: Acts of Union create the Kingdom of Great Britain
events.detail: England and Scotland had shared a monarch since 1603 but kept separate parliaments. Scotland's attempt to found its own colony at Darien in Central America in the late 1690s ended in disaster, costing a large share of Scottish capital and helping persuade its leaders to accept union. Both parliaments passed Acts of Union, and on 1 May 1707 the two kingdoms became a single state, the Kingdom of Great Britain, with Queen Anne as its sovereign and one parliament at Westminster. Scots gained full access to English trade and colonies, and from then on the empire was British rather than English.

events.text: Treaty of Utrecht: Gibraltar, Menorca, Newfoundland and Acadia gained
events.detail: The War of the Spanish Succession was fought largely to stop France and Spain uniting under one Bourbon king. In the Peace of Utrecht, signed in 1713, Britain did well: Spain ceded the strategic ports of Gibraltar and Menorca, and France ceded Nova Scotia (Acadia), its claims to Newfoundland, lands around Hudson Bay and its half of Saint Kitts. Britain also won the Asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spain's American colonies. The treaty made Britain the leading commercial power in Europe and strengthened its hold on North America and the Mediterranean.

events.text: East India Company victory at Plassey brings Bengal under its control
events.detail: The British East India Company traded in Bengal, India's richest province, whose Nawab, Siraj ud-Daulah, had seized its base at Calcutta in 1756. A Company force under Robert Clive retook the city and then plotted with the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar. On 23 June 1757 at Plassey, Clive's army of about 3,000 faced a Bengal army of around 50,000, but Mir Jafar's troops held back and the Nawab's army broke. Mir Jafar was made nawab as a Company puppet. Bengal came under the Company's de facto control, the beginning of British rule in India.

events.text: Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years' War with large gains
events.detail: The Seven Years' War (1756–63) was a global struggle between Britain and France, fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa and India. Britain won a string of victories and captured Canada, French islands in the Caribbean, French trading posts in India and Spanish Havana and Manila. By the Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 February 1763, Britain gave back some conquests but gained much of France's possessions in North America, including Canada, and Spain ceded Florida. The treaty marked the beginning of an era of British dominance outside Europe, and Britain now held all of eastern North America.

events.text: Peace of Paris recognises the independence of the United States
events.detail: Disputes over taxation and self-government led thirteen British colonies in North America to rebel in 1775 and declare independence in 1776. With help from France, the Americans forced a British army to surrender at Yorktown in 1781, and the British government fell. Peace talks began in Paris in 1782, and on 3 September 1783 the Treaty of Paris recognised the independence of the United States, with land stretching west to the Mississippi River. Britain lost its most populous colonies, but kept Canada, and turned its attention increasingly to Asia, Africa and the Pacific.

events.text: First Fleet founds a penal colony at Sydney
events.detail: After losing the American colonies, Britain needed somewhere new to send convicts, and the naturalist Joseph Banks, who had sailed with James Cook along Australia's east coast in 1770, urged a colony at Botany Bay. The First Fleet of eleven ships under Captain Arthur Phillip left Portsmouth on 13 May 1787 with over 1,400 convicts, marines, sailors and officials. It reached Botany Bay on 18 January 1788, but Phillip chose Port Jackson to the north instead, arriving there on 26 January 1788 and founding a settlement at Sydney Cove. The penal colony of New South Wales was the start of British settlement in Australia, which spread across the continent and devastated its Aboriginal peoples.

events.text: Treaty of Nanking: Hong Kong Island ceded by China
events.detail: British merchants smuggled opium from India into China to pay for tea, and when the Qing government enforced its ban by seizing British merchants' opium stocks in 1839, Britain went to war. British warships and troops defeated Qing forces along the coast and up the Yangtze, and threatened Nanjing. On 29 August 1842, aboard HMS Cornwallis, China signed the Treaty of Nanking: it paid an indemnity, opened five treaty ports to British trade, and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in perpetuity. Hong Kong became a key British base and trading port in East Asia, and remained British until 1997.

events.text: After the 1857 rebellion, the Crown takes direct rule of India
events.detail: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began as a mutiny of the East India Company's Indian soldiers and spread across northern India before British forces crushed it. The British government decided the Company could no longer be trusted to rule. The Government of India Act, passed on 2 August 1858, abolished the Company's rule and transferred its territories, armies and powers to the Crown, with a Secretary of State for India in London and a viceroy in India. Queen Victoria's rule over India, the British Raj, lasted until 1947 and made India the centrepiece of the empire.

events.text: British occupation of Egypt
events.detail: Egypt was nominally part of the Ottoman Empire, but its ruler, the Khedive, owed huge debts to European banks, and the Suez Canal, opened in 1869, was Britain's main route to India. In 1881 an army officer, Ahmed 'Urabi, led a nationalist movement that took power. In July 1882 the British fleet bombarded Alexandria, and an army of over 40,000 under Garnet Wolseley landed in the Suez Canal zone and crushed 'Urabi's forces at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September. Britain occupied Egypt, ruling it in practice for decades while leaving the Khedive in place.

events.text: Empire at its greatest extent, enlarged by League of Nations mandates
events.detail: After the First World War the colonies of Germany and lands of the Ottoman Empire were shared out among the victors as League of Nations mandates. Britain gained control of Palestine, Transjordan, Iraq, Tanganyika and parts of Cameroon and Togoland, while the Dominions took others. By 1920 the British Empire covered about 35.5 million km², roughly a quarter of the world's land, and in 1913 it had ruled some 412 million people, 23 per cent of the world's population. It was the largest empire in history, though nationalist movements in Ireland, India and Egypt were already challenging it.

events.text: Statute of Westminster makes the Dominions self-governing
events.detail: The Dominions of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Newfoundland and the Irish Free State had long governed themselves at home, and their sacrifices in the First World War strengthened demands for equal status. At the Imperial Conference of 1926 the Balfour Declaration described Britain and the Dominions as equal, autonomous communities. The Statute of Westminster, passed on 11 December 1931, put this into law, removing nearly all of the British Parliament's power to legislate for the Dominions. The Dominions became independent states linked by loyalty to the Crown, and the empire began to turn into the Commonwealth.

events.text: India and Pakistan become independent on 15 August
events.detail: The Indian independence movement, led by the Indian National Congress and figures such as Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, had grown in strength, and after the Second World War Britain could no longer hold India. With the Muslim League demanding a separate state, British India was divided along religious lines. At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 the independent dominions of India and Pakistan came into existence. Partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people, and somewhere between 200,000 and 2 million died in the violence. The loss of India, the empire's largest possession, began the rapid end of British rule in Asia and Africa.

events.text: Suez Crisis exposes Britain's decline as a world power
events.detail: In July 1956 Egypt's President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, still largely controlled by British and French shareholders. France, and then Britain, secretly agreed with Israel that it would invade Egypt, giving them a pretext to step in, as later revealed in the Protocol of Sèvres. Israel attacked on 29 October, and after issuing an ultimatum, Britain and France joined in on 31 October, later landing troops at Port Said. Under heavy pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Nations, they quickly halted and withdrew. The crisis showed that Britain could no longer act as a great power without American support, and it sped up decolonisation.

events.text: Hong Kong handed over to China
events.detail: Hong Kong Island had been ceded to Britain in 1842 and Kowloon in 1860, but most of the territory, the New Territories, was leased from China in 1898 for 99 years. With the lease due to expire, Britain and China signed the Sino-British Joint Declaration in 1984, agreeing that the whole colony would return to China under the principle of 'one country, two systems'. At midnight on 1 July 1997 sovereignty passed to the People's Republic of China, in a ceremony attended by Prince Charles and the last governor, Chris Patten. Although fourteen small overseas territories remain British, the handover symbolised for many the end of the British Empire.

name: Qing China
summary: Nurhaci united the Jurchen (Manchu) tribes as the Later Jin in 1616, and his son Hong Taiji renamed the state Qing in 1636; in 1644 Manchu armies entered Beijing and went on to conquer all of Ming China, Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. At its peak around 1790 the Qing ruled roughly 14.7 million km², but the Opium Wars, the Taiping Rebellion, unequal treaties and defeat by Japan weakened it, and the 1911 revolution brought the abdication of the last emperor in 1912.

events.text: Manchu victory over the Ming at Sarhu
events.detail: The Qing began as the Later Jin, a state founded in 1616 by Nurhaci, a Jurchen chieftain who had united most Jurchen tribes and organised them into the Eight Banners. In 1618 he declared war on the Ming, and in spring 1619 the Ming sent a large army, with Korean (Joseon) allies, in four columns to destroy his capital at Hetu Ala. Nurhaci concentrated his cavalry and defeated the columns one by one around Sarhu, in today's Liaoning, over a few days. The victory gave the Jurchens the initiative in the northeast, and within a few years they took Shenyang and most of Liaodong.

events.text: Hong Taiji renames his state the Great Qing
events.detail: Nurhaci's son Hong Taiji, who took power in 1626, conquered Inner Mongolia and the rest of Manchuria and invaded Korea, which became a Qing tributary. In 1635 he renamed his people from Jurchen to 'Manchu', and in 1636 he proclaimed himself emperor and changed the name of his dynasty from 'Great Jin' to 'Great Qing'. The Qing now claimed to rule as a rival to the Ming, with its capital at Mukden (Shenyang), and Hong Taiji prepared the way for the conquest of China.

events.text: Qing and Wu Sangui defeat Li Zicheng at Shanhai Pass; Beijing taken
events.detail: In April 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng captured Beijing and the last Ming emperor killed himself. The Ming general Wu Sangui, guarding the Great Wall at Shanhai Pass, turned to the Manchus for help. On 27 May 1644 Li's army attacked the pass, and the combined forces of Wu Sangui and the Qing regent Dorgon routed it. Li abandoned Beijing, and the Qing entered the city on 6 June; the young Shunzhi Emperor was enthroned there as ruler of China. The battle opened China proper to the Manchus, who spent the next two decades conquering the Ming lands to the south.

events.text: Revolt of the Three Feudatories crushed after eight years
events.detail: To reward Wu Sangui and two other Chinese generals who had helped conquer the south, the Qing gave them vast hereditary fiefs in Yunnan, Guangdong and Fujian. By the 1670s these 'Three Feudatories' were almost independent and very costly. When the Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish them in 1673, Wu Sangui rebelled, and the other two feudatories and the Zheng regime on Taiwan joined him, taking much of southern China. The Qing gradually won back the provinces, and the revolt was crushed in 1681. Kangxi's victory secured Qing control over all of southern China.

events.text: Zheng regime on Taiwan surrenders to the Qing
events.detail: After the Ming fell, the loyalist commander Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) drove the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and founded the Kingdom of Tungning there, which kept fighting the Qing. In July 1683 the Qing admiral Shi Lang attacked with a large fleet and destroyed the Zheng navy at the Battle of Penghu, killing or capturing thousands of men. With its fleet gone, the Zheng government under the young Zheng Keshuang surrendered on 5 September 1683. Taiwan was brought into the Qing empire for the first time, ending the last organised Ming loyalist resistance.

events.text: Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia
events.detail: As Russian explorers and Cossacks pushed into the Amur River valley, they clashed with the Qing, who besieged the Russian fort at Albazin in 1685–86. In 1689 envoys of the Kangxi Emperor and the Russian tsars met at Nerchinsk and, using Latin with Jesuit priests as interpreters, signed the first formal treaty China ever made with a Western power. Russia gave up the Amur basin, and the border was set along the Argun River and the Stanovoy Mountains, while Russia gained trading rights. The treaty secured the Qing's northern frontier in Manchuria for about 170 years.

events.text: Conquest of Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin (Xinjiang) completed
events.detail: For decades the Dzungar Khanate, the last great nomadic empire of the Mongol Oirats, had fought the Qing for control of Mongolia, Tibet and Central Asia. In the 1750s, amid a Dzungar succession crisis, the Qianlong Emperor sent armies that destroyed the khanate; a large part of the Dzungar population died in the slaughter and epidemics that followed, now described as a genocide. Qing forces then took the Tarim Basin, and by 1759 the conquest was complete. The new region became known as Xinjiang ('new frontier'), adding a vast territory in Central Asia to the empire.

events.text: c. 1790: Qing at its greatest extent, about 14.7 million km²
events.detail: Under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors, the Qing fought a long series of wars, including Qianlong's 'Ten Great Campaigns', on its Inner Asian and southern frontiers. By about 1790 the empire stretched from Manchuria and Mongolia to Xinjiang and Tibet, about twice the size of the Ming state, and by scholarly estimates covered some 14.7 million km². It was the largest territory of any Chinese dynasty and laid the territorial base of modern China. In peace its population rose to around 400 million, but taxes stayed low and fixed, and costly wars and corruption soon strained the state.

events.text: Treaty of Nanking ends the First Opium War; Hong Kong Island ceded
events.detail: British merchants smuggled opium from India into China to pay for tea, and when the Qing official Lin Zexu enforced the ban by seizing their opium stocks in 1839, Britain went to war. British warships defeated Qing forces along the coast and up the Yangtze, threatening Nanjing. On 29 August 1842 the Qing signed the Treaty of Nanking, paying an indemnity, opening five treaty ports to British merchants and ceding Hong Kong Island to Britain. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties' that forced China open to Western powers and began what Chinese call the century of humiliation.

events.text: Taiping Rebellion breaks out (crushed 1864)
events.detail: In the 1840s Hong Xiuquan, a failed civil-service candidate who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, founded a religious movement in southern China. In late 1850 his followers rose in revolt and proclaimed the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom; in 1853 they captured Nanjing and made it their capital. For over a decade they held much of the rich Yangtze valley. Regional armies raised by officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, later helped by Western-led forces, finally retook Nanjing in 1864. Estimates of the dead range from 20 to 100 million, and the war left the Qing government badly weakened.

events.text: Outer Manchuria ceded to Russia (Convention of Peking)
events.detail: In the Second Opium War (1856–60) British and French forces fought the Qing again, captured Beijing in 1860 and burned the Old Summer Palace. Russia, which had already won the north bank of the Amur by the Treaty of Aigun in 1858, offered to mediate. In the Convention of Peking, signed in 1860, China also ceded Kowloon to Britain, and the Russian envoy Nikolay Ignatyev obtained the land between the Ussuri River and the Pacific. China lost all of Outer Manchuria, about 400,000 km² by this treaty alone, and its access to the Sea of Japan.

events.text: Treaty of Shimonoseki: Taiwan and Penghu ceded to Japan
events.detail: Japan, modernising rapidly after 1868, and China clashed over influence in Korea, a Qing tributary state. In the war of 1894–95 Japan's army and navy defeated the Qing forces, defeating the Beiyang Fleet at the Yalu River and taking Port Arthur and Weihaiwei. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki, signed on 17 April 1895, China recognised Korea's independence, paid an indemnity of 200 million taels, and ceded Taiwan, the Penghu Islands and the Liaodong Peninsula to Japan. Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to return Liaodong a week later. The defeat by a smaller Asian neighbour showed the weakness of the Qing and set off a scramble by foreign powers for concessions in China.

events.text: Boxer Rebellion; foreign armies occupy Beijing
events.detail: Anger at foreign influence and Christian missionaries fed a movement in northern China known in the West as the Boxers, whose followers attacked missionaries and Chinese Christians. In June 1900 the Qing court backed them and declared war on the foreign powers; Chinese troops and Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing from 20 June to 14 August. An Eight-Nation Alliance of foreign armies relieved the legations and occupied Beijing, and the Empress Dowager Cixi fled to Xi'an. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver and foreign troops in Beijing, further weakening the dynasty.

events.text: Wuchang Uprising starts the Xinhai Revolution (abdication Feb 1912)
events.detail: By 1911 many Chinese blamed the Manchu Qing for China's weakness, and revolutionary groups such as Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui had spread their ideas in the army. On 10 October 1911 units of the New Army rose in revolt at Wuchang, in today's Wuhan, starting the 1911 (Xinhai) Revolution, and one province after another renounced the Qing. On 1 January 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed at Nanjing with Sun as provisional president. The court turned to Yuan Shikai, who negotiated the abdication of the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor (Puyi) on 12 February 1912, ending 267 years of Qing rule and over two millennia of imperial rule in China.

name: Maratha Empire
summary: Shivaji, crowned Chhatrapati in 1674, carved a Maratha kingdom out of the Deccan and survived a long war with Aurangzeb (1680–1707). Under Chhatrapati Shahu the Peshwas of Pune led the confederacy north across Malwa to Delhi and Attock, reaching a peak of roughly 2.5 million km² around 1760, until the Afghan victory at Panipat in 1761. The Marathas recovered Delhi in 1771 but were defeated by the British East India Company in three wars, the last ending in 1818.

events.text: Shivaji's southern campaign takes Gingee and Vellore
events.detail: Shivaji had carved out a Maratha kingdom in western India from the lands of Bijapur and the Mughals, and was crowned Chhatrapati (king) in 1674. In 1677 he visited Hyderabad and made a treaty with the Qutb Shahi sultan of Golconda to oppose the Mughals jointly. Backed by Golconda's artillery and money, he invaded the south with a large army of cavalry and infantry and seized the forts of Gingee and Vellore, along with much of his half-brother Venkoji's lands. The campaign gave the Marathas a vast territory on the Mysore plateau and the Madras Carnatic, and Gingee later served as their refuge from the Mughals.

events.text: Sambhaji captured and executed by the Mughals
events.detail: After Shivaji's death in 1680 his son Sambhaji became Chhatrapati and fought the huge Mughal army that Aurangzeb had brought into the Deccan. Mughal pressure grew, key commanders died and troops deserted. In February 1689 Sambhaji and 25 of his advisers were captured by the Mughal commander Muqarrab Khan at Sangameshwar. He was paraded in humiliation, tortured and executed on Aurangzeb's orders on 11 March 1689. The Maratha kingdom fell into disarray, and Sambhaji's young son Shahu was held captive by the Mughals, but his half-brother Rajaram took the throne, moved the capital far south to Gingee and continued the war.

events.text: Shahu released after Aurangzeb's death and claims the throne
events.detail: Shahu, Sambhaji's son, had grown up as a captive at the Mughal court since 1689. After Aurangzeb died in 1707, his son Azam Shah released Shahu, hoping to set off a civil war among the Marathas. Shahu's aunt Tarabai, ruling in the name of her own son, denounced him as an impostor, and the two sides fought for the throne. Shahu won wide support and was crowned Chhatrapati at Satara on 12 January 1708. The split weakened the Marathas for a time, but under Shahu, who reigned until 1749, the state grew from a regional kingdom into an empire.

events.text: Shahu appoints Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa
events.detail: Shahu needed capable ministers to defeat Tarabai's faction and deal with the Mughals. On 16 November 1713 he appointed Balaji Vishwanath, a Chitpavan Brahmin administrator, as Peshwa (chief minister). Balaji won over powerful Maratha commanders to Shahu's side, and in 1718–19 he helped the Sayyid brothers, kingmakers at the Mughal court, march on Delhi in return for Maratha rights to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi (shares of revenue) in the Deccan. The office of Peshwa became hereditary in his family, and from then on the Peshwas, based in Pune, were the real rulers of the Maratha state.

events.text: Baji Rao I defeats the Nizam at Palkhed
events.detail: Balaji Vishwanath's son Baji Rao I became Peshwa in 1720 and soon clashed with Asaf Jah I, the Nizam of Hyderabad, who disputed the Maratha right to collect revenue in the Deccan. In 1728 Baji Rao's fast-moving cavalry outmanoeuvred the Nizam's army and trapped it near Palkhed, cutting its supplies and communications. Forced to make peace, the Nizam signed the Treaty of Mungi Shevgaon on 6 March 1728, recognising Shahu as king and the Maratha right to collect taxes in the Deccan. The campaign is often praised as a masterpiece of strategy, and it made the Marathas the dominant power in the Deccan.

events.text: Baji Rao I raids Delhi and defeats the Mughals at Bhopal
events.detail: Baji Rao I expanded Maratha power north into Malwa, Gujarat and Bundelkhand, demanding revenue from Mughal provinces. In 1737 he raided as far as the outskirts of Delhi and defeated a Mughal army there, the high point of his military career. On his way back, the Nizam, called in by the Mughal emperor, intercepted him with a combined army near Bhopal. The Marathas surrounded the Nizam's forces, cut off their water and supplies, and won the Battle of Bhopal on 24 December 1737. The victory showed that the Mughals could no longer protect even the lands near their capital.

events.text: Treaty of Bhopal confirms Maratha control of Malwa
events.detail: Trapped and short of supplies after the Battle of Bhopal, the Nizam had to accept Baji Rao's terms. In the Treaty of Bhopal, signed on 7 January 1738, the Mughals ceded the large province of Malwa in central India to the Marathas and agreed to pay 50 lakh rupees as war expenses. Malwa became a Maratha territory, later ruled by Maratha families such as the Holkars and Scindias. By the time Baji Rao died in 1740, the Maratha Empire had reached its greatest extent yet and was one of the largest powers in India.

events.text: Marathas win at Attock and take Peshawar
events.detail: After the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani plundered Delhi in 1756, the Peshwa's brother Raghunath Rao led a Maratha army north. In August 1757 he took Delhi, defeating the Afghan garrison, and then pushed into the Punjab, taking Lahore. In 1758 the Marathas won at Attock on the Indus, and on 8 May 1758 they defeated the Afghan troops at Peshawar and captured the city. Maratha power now stretched to the borders of Afghanistan, its furthest reach, but the advance provoked Ahmad Shah Durrani, who returned to India to fight them.

events.text: Crushing defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.detail: Ahmad Shah Durrani invaded India again, backed by the Rohillas and the Nawab of Awadh, to drive the Marathas from the north. A large Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau, with the Peshwa's son Vishwasrao and tens of thousands of pilgrims and camp followers, marched north to meet him. On 14 January 1761, at Panipat north of Delhi, the Afghans crushed the Marathas; Sadashivrao and Vishwasrao were killed, along with tens of thousands of soldiers, and many non-combatants were massacred afterwards. Maratha authority in northern India collapsed for a decade.

events.text: Mahadaji Shinde recaptures Delhi
events.detail: After Panipat, the Marathas slowly rebuilt their power in the north under leaders such as Mahadaji Shinde (Scindia) of Gwalior. In early 1771, ten years after Panipat, Mahadaji recaptured Delhi, and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, who had spent six years in the fort at Allahabad, returned to his capital under Maratha escort. Shah Alam became in effect a Maratha puppet. Mahadaji was later made deputy regent of the empire, and the Marathas again controlled much of northern India, now competing with the British East India Company.

events.text: Treaty of Salbai ends the First Anglo-Maratha War
events.detail: In the 1770s a succession dispute among the Peshwas led the former Peshwa Raghunath Rao to seek British help, starting the First Anglo-Maratha War. The Marathas held their own, forcing a British force to surrender at Wadgaon, and the war ended without major British gains. On 17 May 1782 Mahadaji Shinde and the Governor-General, Warren Hastings, signed the Treaty of Salbai, under which the Company kept Salsette and Broach, pensioned off Raghunath Rao and recognised Madhavrao II as Peshwa. The treaty brought twenty years of peace with the British, during which the Marathas remained the leading power in India.

events.text: Victory over the Nizam at Kharda
events.detail: The Nizam of Hyderabad had long disputed the Marathas' claims to revenue in the Deccan. In 1795 the Maratha chiefs, united for the last time under the command of Parshuram Bhau Patwardhan, marched against him and won a decisive victory at Kharda on 11 March 1795. After a siege of his camp at Kharda fort, the Nizam made peace in April 1795, agreeing to pay a large indemnity and cede the territories of Daulatabad, Aurangabad and Solapur. It was the last great victory won jointly by the whole Maratha Confederacy, which soon fell into rivalry among its chiefs.

events.text: Peshwa accepts British protection in the Treaty of Bassein
events.detail: After the deaths of strong leaders such as Mahadaji Shinde in 1794, the Maratha chiefs quarrelled. In 1802 Yashwantrao Holkar of Indore defeated the forces of Peshwa Baji Rao II and the Scindias at the Battle of Poona, and the Peshwa fled to the British. On 31 December 1802 at Bassein (Vasai) he signed a treaty accepting British protection: he agreed to host Company troops, exclude other Europeans from his service and conduct his foreign relations through the British. The Treaty of Bassein was a decisive step in the break-up of the Maratha Empire and soon led to war.

events.text: Second Anglo-Maratha War against the East India Company (to 1805)
events.detail: The Scindias of Gwalior and the Bhonsles of Nagpur refused to accept the Treaty of Bassein, and war with the East India Company broke out in August 1803. British armies under Arthur Wellesley (later Duke of Wellington) and Gerard Lake won major battles, including Assaye in the Deccan and Laswari in the north, and took Delhi, bringing the Mughal emperor under British protection. Holkar joined the war later. By 1805 the Marathas had lost large territories, including the regions around Delhi and parts of Gujarat, to direct Company rule, and the British were now the strongest power in India.

events.text: Third Anglo-Maratha War: Baji Rao II surrenders; Peshwa rule ends
events.detail: In 1817 Peshwa Baji Rao II, resenting British control, rose against the East India Company, supported by the Bhonsles of Nagpur and the Holkars of Indore, while the Company also campaigned against the Pindari raiders. Maratha armies were defeated at Koregaon and other battles, and the Peshwa was pursued across the Deccan until he surrendered in June 1818. He was pensioned off to a small estate at Bithur, near Kanpur, and the office of Peshwa was abolished. Most of his lands became part of the Bombay Presidency, and the end of the Maratha Empire left the British masters of most of India.

name: First French Empire (Napoleonic)
summary: Napoleon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French in May 1804 and crowned that December. Victories over Austria, Prussia and Russia (1805–1807) let him annex territory directly to France and ring it with satellite kingdoms and confederations run by his relatives and allies, a system at its height around 1810–1812. The disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812 and defeat at Leipzig in 1813 broke it, and he abdicated in April 1814; his return in the Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in 1815.

events.text: Victory over Austria and Russia at Austerlitz; Treaty of Pressburg
events.detail: Napoleon Bonaparte, who had crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804, faced a Third Coalition of Britain, Austria and Russia. After trapping an Austrian army at Ulm, he met the combined Russian and Austrian armies near Austerlitz in Moravia on 2 December 1805, with Emperors Alexander I and Francis II present, so that it was called the Battle of the Three Emperors. Napoleon lured the allies into attacking his weakened right and then broke their centre, winning a crushing victory. By the Peace of Pressburg on 26 December, Austria gave up Venetia, Istria and Dalmatia to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and Tyrol to Bavaria, and paid 40 million francs.

events.text: Confederation of the Rhine formed; Prussia crushed at Jena–Auerstedt
events.detail: After Austerlitz, Napoleon reorganised western Germany. On 12 July 1806, 16 German states signed the treaty creating the Confederation of the Rhine, a league of French allies with Napoleon as its 'Protector', and on 6 August Francis II dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, which had existed since the Middle Ages. Alarmed, Prussia went to war, but on 14 October 1806 Napoleon at Jena and Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout at Auerstedt destroyed the two Prussian armies on the same day. The French soon entered Berlin, and Napoleon now dominated all of Germany.

events.text: Treaties of Tilsit; Duchy of Warsaw and Kingdom of Westphalia created
events.detail: Napoleon pursued the Prussians and their Russian allies east, and in June 1807 he defeated the Russian army at Friedland. On 7 July he met Tsar Alexander I on a raft in the Neman River at Tilsit and made peace, and on 9 July a second treaty was imposed on Prussia, which lost about half of its territory. From these lands Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw, ruled by his ally the King of Saxony, and the Kingdom of Westphalia, under his brother Jérôme. Russia agreed to join his blockade of British trade. Napoleon's power in Europe was at its height.

events.text: French invasion of the Iberian Peninsula; Joseph made King of Spain
events.detail: To enforce his blockade of Britain, Napoleon sent troops through Spain to occupy Portugal in 1807, and in 1808 he turned on his Spanish ally. He forced King Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII to give up the throne and made his brother Joseph King of Spain. On 2 May 1808 the people of Madrid rose against the French, starting the Peninsular War, in which Spanish armies and guerrillas, with British and Portuguese forces later led by Wellington, fought the French for six years. The war tied down large French armies and cost an estimated million or more military and civilian lives.

events.text: Treaty of Schönbrunn after victory over Austria; Warsaw enlarged
events.detail: While Napoleon was busy in Spain, Austria went to war again in 1809, hoping to reverse its losses of 1805. Napoleon took Vienna and defeated the Austrians decisively at Wagram on 5–6 July. By the Treaty of Schönbrunn, signed on 14 October 1809, Austria ceded Salzburg to Bavaria, lost its access to the Adriatic when its coastal lands became the French-ruled Illyrian Provinces, and gave West Galicia to the Duchy of Warsaw, which grew much larger. Austria, weakened but still a great power, made peace with France, and in 1810 Napoleon married the Austrian emperor's daughter, Marie Louise.

events.text: Kingdom of Holland annexed directly to France
events.detail: In 1806 Napoleon had made his brother Louis King of Holland. Louis tried to protect Dutch interests and did not strictly enforce the Continental System, Napoleon's ban on trade with Britain, so smuggling continued. Losing patience, Napoleon sent troops, and French forces took Amsterdam in early July 1810; Louis abdicated on 1 July in favour of his son, and on 9 July 1810 the kingdom was annexed directly to the French Empire. The Netherlands were now ruled directly from Paris, and by 1812 the French Empire had grown to 130 departments with more than 44 million people.

events.text: Grande Armée invades Russia in June; catastrophic retreat
events.detail: Russia had stopped enforcing Napoleon's blockade of Britain, and Napoleon decided to force it back into line. On 24 June 1812 the Grande Armée, a multinational force of more than 600,000 men, crossed the Neman River into Russia. The Russians retreated, fought a bloody battle at Borodino, and abandoned Moscow, which Napoleon entered on 14 September to find it deserted and set ablaze on the orders of its governor. Alexander I refused to negotiate, and in October the French began a disastrous retreat through the Russian winter, harried by Cossacks. Most of the army was lost, and the campaign cost around a million military and civilian lives.

events.text: Defeat at Leipzig; Confederation of the Rhine dissolved
events.detail: After the disaster in Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden joined Russia and Britain in the Sixth Coalition. Napoleon rebuilt his army and won early battles in Germany, but on 16–19 October 1813 the coalition armies trapped him at Leipzig in the 'Battle of the Nations', the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, involving about 560,000 soldiers. Saxon and other German troops changed sides during the fighting, and Napoleon was defeated and retreated across the Rhine. The Confederation of the Rhine dissolved, and France lost control of all its territory east of the Rhine.

events.text: Paris capitulates; Napoleon abdicates at Fontainebleau
events.detail: In early 1814 the coalition armies invaded France itself. Napoleon won several battles but could not stop their advance on the capital. On 30 March 1814 Russian, Austrian, Prussian and other allied troops attacked Paris, and after a day of fighting Marshals Marmont and Mortier agreed to a ceasefire; the French evacuated the city on 31 March, and the allies entered it. Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau, and by the treaty agreed there on 11 April he was sent into exile on Elba. His rule as Emperor of the French was over, and the Bourbon King Louis XVIII took the throne.

name: Empire of Japan
summary: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 created a modernising, centralised Japan that absorbed Hokkaido and the Ryukyu Islands and then won Taiwan from China (1895), southern Sakhalin and the Kwantung lease from Russia (1905), and Korea (1910). Seizing Manchuria in 1931 and invading China in 1937, it struck at the United States and European colonies in 1941 and briefly ruled an empire of about 7.4 million km² in 1942, before defeat and surrender in 1945.

events.text: Meiji Restoration restores imperial rule
events.detail: Since 1603 Japan had been ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns, military rulers who kept the emperor as a figurehead and limited contact with the outside world. After the American Perry Expedition of the 1850s forced Japan to open its ports, the shogunate faced economic and political crises and foreign pressure, and the domains of Satsuma and Chōshū led an alliance against it. On 3 January 1868 Emperor Meiji declared political power restored to the imperial house. The new government abolished the feudal domains and the samurai class and set out to industrialise and modernise Japan, creating the Empire of Japan.

events.text: Shogunate loyalists of the Ezo Republic surrender at Hakodate
events.detail: Supporters of the Tokugawa fought on after the restoration in the Boshin War. When the new government's forces took the shogun's capital, Edo, the navy commander Enomoto Takeaki sailed north with part of the shogunate's fleet to the island of Ezo (Hokkaido). There his followers set up the Ezo Republic in January 1869, a short-lived state in which samurai elected their leaders. Imperial forces landed on the island and besieged Hakodate, and the republic was dissolved on 27 June 1869 after five months. Its surrender ended the Boshin War and left the Meiji government in control of all Japan, including Hokkaido.

events.text: Ryukyu Kingdom abolished and annexed as Okinawa Prefecture
events.detail: The Ryukyu Kingdom, a chain of islands south of Japan, had long sent tribute to China while also being dominated by the Japanese domain of Satsuma. The Meiji government made it the Ryukyu Domain in 1872, with King Shō Tai as a vassal, and pressed it to cut its ties with China. In 1879 Japan abolished the kingdom and annexed it as Okinawa Prefecture, one of Japan's home prefectures. China protested, and talks brokered by the former US president Ulysses S. Grant led nowhere. The annexation extended Japan's territory south, towards Taiwan.

events.text: Treaty of Shimonoseki: Taiwan and Penghu won from China
events.detail: Japan and Qing China competed for influence in Korea, a Chinese tributary state. In the war of 1894–95 the modernised Japanese army and navy defeated Chinese forces in Korea, destroyed the Beiyang Fleet's power at the Yalu River and took Port Arthur and Weihaiwei. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki, signed on 17 April 1895, China recognised Korea's independence, paid an indemnity of 200 million taels and ceded Taiwan, the Penghu Islands and the Liaodong Peninsula. Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to give back Liaodong a week later. Taiwan became Japan's first colony, and Japan emerged as a major power in East Asia.

events.text: Treaty of Portsmouth: southern Sakhalin and Kwantung lease from Russia
events.detail: Japan and Russia both wanted control of Korea and Manchuria, and in February 1904 Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur. Japan won a series of victories, including the capture of Port Arthur, the land battle of Mukden and the destruction of Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in May 1905. US President Theodore Roosevelt mediated peace talks, and on 5 September 1905 the Treaty of Portsmouth recognised Japan's dominance in Korea and gave it Russia's lease on the Liaodong Peninsula (the Kwantung Leased Territory), the South Manchuria Railway and the southern half of Sakhalin. The victory made Japan a great power and damaged Russia's prestige in Europe.

events.text: Korea annexed
events.detail: After the war with Russia, Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and took control of its foreign affairs and army. Korean resistance continued, while Japanese leaders such as Itō Hirobumi pressed for a full 'merger'. On 22 August 1910 representatives of the two empires signed the Japan–Korea Annexation Treaty, which came into force on 29 August, and the Korean Empire was abolished. Korea became a Japanese colony, ruled by a governor-general, for 35 years until Japan's defeat in 1945. The annexation gave Japan a foothold on the Asian mainland.

events.text: Japan enters the First World War against Germany
events.detail: Japan was allied with Britain, and when the First World War broke out it saw a chance to seize Germany's possessions in Asia. Japan sent Germany an ultimatum and declared war on 23 August 1914. Japanese troops besieged the German base at Tsingtao (Qingdao) in China, which surrendered on 7 November, and the navy seized Germany's Pacific islands, the Marianas, Carolines and Marshalls, with little resistance. In 1915 Japan pressed its Twenty-One Demands on China. After the war Japan kept the islands as a League of Nations mandate, extending its empire across the western Pacific.

events.text: Mukden Incident: Japanese army seizes Manchuria
events.detail: Japan's Kwantung Army guarded the South Manchuria Railway, and its officers wanted to seize all of Manchuria, rich in coal and farmland, from China. On 18 September 1931 Japanese officers secretly set off a small explosion on the railway near Mukden (Shenyang) and blamed Chinese troops. Using this as a pretext, and despite Tokyo's attempts to curb the army's insubordination, the army attacked Chinese forces and within months occupied all of Manchuria. The invasion showed that the army could drive Japanese policy, and it began fourteen years of Japanese aggression in China.

events.text: Puppet state of Manchukuo proclaimed
events.detail: To give its conquest a show of legitimacy, Japan created a new state in Manchuria. On 1 March 1932 Manchukuo was proclaimed, with Puyi, the last Qing emperor of China who had abdicated as a child in 1912, as its nominal head; in 1934 he was made emperor. Real power lay with Japanese officials and the Kwantung Army. When the League of Nations endorsed the Lytton Report, which called Manchukuo a Japanese puppet, Japan withdrew from the League in 1933. Manchukuo, enlarged by the annexation of Rehe in 1933, became an industrial base and a large addition to Japan's sphere of control.

events.text: Full-scale war with China begins
events.detail: Japanese troops based near Beijing clashed with Chinese troops at the Marco Polo Bridge (Lugou Bridge) on the night of 7 July 1937. Neither side backed down, and the incident escalated into a full-scale Japanese invasion of China. After a long battle for Shanghai, Japanese forces captured the Chinese capital, Nanjing, in December 1937 and carried out the Nanjing Massacre. Japan occupied much of eastern China, but the Chinese government retreated inland and kept fighting. The war in China, which killed millions, tied down much of Japan's army until 1945.

events.text: Attack on Pearl Harbor; war with the United States and Britain
events.detail: Japan, still heavily dependent on American oil and other imports, decided to seize the resources of Southeast Asia, held by the United States, Britain and the Netherlands. On 7 December 1941 Japanese carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging many battleships and killing 2,403 Americans. Within hours Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong. The United States and Britain declared war. The attack brought the US into the Second World War and began the Pacific War.

events.text: Empire at its greatest extent, about 7.4 million km²
events.detail: In the months after Pearl Harbor, Japanese forces overran Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines, Burma and many Pacific islands. In 1942 the empire and the lands it occupied covered about 7.4 million km², stretching from Manchuria and much of China to the borders of India and deep into the Pacific. But in June 1942 Japan lost four fleet carriers at the Battle of Midway, its navy's first decisive defeat and the turning point of the war. After Midway and the long fight for Guadalcanal, Japan was forced onto the defensive and steadily pushed back.

events.text: Atomic bombings and Soviet invasion; surrender signed 2 September
events.detail: By mid-1945 Japan's navy was largely destroyed and its cities devastated by bombing, but its leaders refused to surrender. On 6 August the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima; on 9 August the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria, and hours later a second bomb destroyed Nagasaki. Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on 15 August, and the Instrument of Surrender was signed aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945. The Soviets took southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, Japan lost its empire overseas, and Allied occupation followed.

name: German Empire
summary: Proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871 after Prussia's victory over France, the German Empire united the German states outside Austria under the Prussian king as emperor. From 1884 it acquired colonies in Africa and the Pacific, the fourth-largest colonial empire of its day, and under Wilhelm II pursued world-power ambitions; defeat in the First World War, despite brief gains in the east in 1918, brought revolution, the emperor's abdication and the loss of all its colonies.

events.text: Empire proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January
events.detail: Prussia, led by its chief minister Otto von Bismarck, had defeated Denmark and Austria and formed the North German Confederation. In 1870–71 Prussia and its allies, including the southern German states, defeated France in the Franco-Prussian War. While German troops were still besieging Paris, on 18 January 1871 the German princes proclaimed King Wilhelm I of Prussia German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. The new empire united the German states, apart from Austria, into a single nation under Prussian leadership, and it quickly became a leading power in Europe.

events.text: Protectorates over South West Africa, Togoland and Kamerun
events.detail: Bismarck had long preferred informal trade to colonies, but German merchants and nationalists pressed for an overseas empire. In 1882 the Bremen merchant Adolf Lüderitz asked for protection for a trading station in South West Africa, and in 1884 Germany declared protectorates there, and in Togoland (July) and Kamerun (August) on the West African coast, with the explorer Gustav Nachtigal raising the flag. Within a few months Germany had become a colonial power in Africa. With German South West Africa (now Namibia), Togoland and Kamerun, Germany began a colonial empire that by 1912 covered about 3.5 million km² in Africa and the Pacific.

events.text: German East Africa established
events.detail: In 1884 the adventurer Carl Peters and his Society for German Colonisation made treaties with chiefs in East Africa, and in 1885 the German government placed these lands under imperial protection, run at first by the German East Africa Company. The company's rule provoked a coastal revolt in 1888, and the German military was sent in to crush it, after which the state took direct control. German East Africa, covering present-day mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, became Germany's largest and most populous colony, almost twice the size of Germany itself, with its capital at Dar es Salaam from 1890.

events.text: Year of three emperors: Wilhelm II succeeds
events.detail: The founding emperor, Wilhelm I, died on 9 March 1888 after a reign of 17 years as emperor. His son, Frederick III, a liberal who might have changed Germany's direction, was already suffering from cancer of the larynx and reigned for only 99 days before he died on 15 June. His 29-year-old son became Emperor Wilhelm II. The 'Year of the Three Emperors' brought to power an ambitious young ruler who would build a powerful navy and follow an erratic foreign policy. Wilhelm II would reign until the empire's collapse in 1918.

events.text: Bismarck dismissed; Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty with Britain
events.detail: Wilhelm II wanted to rule personally and clashed with the 75-year-old Bismarck, who had dominated German politics for nearly three decades. On 18 March 1890 Bismarck resigned at the emperor's insistence and was replaced as chancellor by Leo von Caprivi. On 1 July 1890 Caprivi's government signed the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty with Britain: Germany gained the North Sea island of Heligoland, needed to protect its naval ports, and the Caprivi Strip linking South West Africa to the Zambezi, while recognising British authority over Zanzibar. The treaty settled colonial borders in Africa, and with Bismarck gone, Wilhelm II increasingly steered German policy himself.

events.text: German forces occupy Jiaozhou Bay (Kiautschou) in China
events.detail: Wilhelm II and his naval planners wanted a base in China for the German navy. On 1 November 1897 two German Catholic missionaries were murdered in Shandong province, and Admiral Otto von Diederichs used the killings as a pretext: on 14 November his squadron landed troops and occupied Jiaozhou Bay. On 6 March 1898 China was forced to lease the bay to Germany for 99 years. Germany built the port and naval base of Tsingtao (Qingdao) there, and the seizure was part of the great powers' scramble for leases and spheres of influence in China.

events.text: Micronesian islands bought from Spain; western Samoa annexed
events.detail: After Spain lost the Philippines and Guam to the United States in 1898, it decided to sell its remaining Pacific islands. By the German–Spanish Treaty of 12 February 1899, Germany bought the Caroline Islands, including Palau, and the Northern Mariana Islands for 25 million pesetas and placed them under German New Guinea. In December 1899 the Tripartite Convention with Britain and the United States ended a civil war in Samoa and divided the islands: Germany took the western islands, and the United States took Tutuila and the eastern islands. Germany's Pacific empire reached its greatest extent.

events.text: Herero War begins in South West Africa, leading to genocide
events.detail: In German South West Africa, settlers had taken much of the land and cattle of the Herero and Nama peoples. On 12 January 1904 the Herero chief Samuel Maharero launched an uprising. After reinforcements arrived from Germany under General Lothar von Trotha, the Herero were surrounded and routed at the Battle of Waterberg in August 1904, and many fled into the Omaheke desert, where most died of thirst and starvation; von Trotha ordered their extermination. The Nama also rose and were crushed. An estimated 40,000 to 80,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama died, in what is now recognised as a genocide.

events.text: First World War; most colonies soon lost to Allied forces
events.detail: When the First World War began in August 1914, Germany's colonies were isolated and lightly defended, and Britain controlled the seas. Togoland surrendered to British and French forces within weeks, Japan took Tsingtao in November, and Japanese, Australian and New Zealand forces seized the Pacific colonies. South African troops conquered South West Africa by July 1915, and Kamerun fell in 1916. Only in German East Africa did General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck's force hold out until after the armistice in 1918. Germany lost nearly all its overseas empire early in the war.

events.text: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March); abdication of Wilhelm II (November)
events.detail: After the Russian Revolution, the Bolshevik government wanted peace at almost any price. By the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918 with Germany and its allies, Russia gave up its claims to Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, most of Belarus and Ukraine, which came under German influence, briefly giving Germany a huge empire in the east. But the German army's last offensives in the west failed, and in the autumn its allies collapsed. Amid naval mutinies and revolution at home, Chancellor Max von Baden announced Wilhelm II's abdication on 9 November 1918; Germany was proclaimed a republic, and the emperor fled to the Netherlands.

name: Soviet Union
summary: Formed in December 1922 by the Bolshevik-ruled republics that emerged from the Russian Civil War, the Soviet Union recovered most of the old empire's lands. The 1939 pact with Nazi Germany let it annex eastern Poland, the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania; it survived the German invasion of 1941, won in 1945 with further gains, and dominated Eastern Europe as a superpower. Economic stagnation, the Afghan war and Gorbachev's reforms led to the collapse of its satellites in 1989 and its own dissolution in December 1991.

events.text: Treaty on the Creation of the USSR approved on 30 December
events.detail: After the Bolsheviks seized power in Russia in 1917 and won the Russian Civil War, several Soviet republics existed side by side, all ruled by the Communist Party. To bind them together, delegations from the Russian SFSR, the Ukrainian SSR, the Byelorussian SSR and the Transcaucasian SFSR approved the Declaration and Treaty on the Creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics on 30 December 1922. The treaty set up a federal state with its government in Moscow. The Soviet Union inherited most of the former Russian Empire's territory and became the world's first communist state, lasting until 1991.

events.text: Death of Lenin; Stalin wins the power struggle
events.detail: Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the Soviet state, was disabled by three strokes in 1922–23 and died on 21 January 1924, aged 53. A struggle for power followed among the party's leaders, including Leon Trotsky, Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev and Nikolai Bukharin. Joseph Stalin, General Secretary of the Communist Party since 1922, used his control of the party apparatus to outmanoeuvre his rivals one by one, and by the late 1920s he ruled the Soviet Union. Under his 'Socialism in One Country' and five-year plans, the country was forcibly industrialised and its farms collectivised, at the cost of millions of lives.

events.text: Pact with Nazi Germany; Soviet invasion of eastern Poland
events.detail: In August 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact, dated 23 August, whose secret protocol divided Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence, including a partition of Poland. A week later Germany invaded Poland, starting the Second World War. On 17 September 1939 the Red Army invaded Poland from the east without a declaration of war, and the two powers divided the country. The Soviet Union annexed eastern Poland, today's western Belarus and western Ukraine, pushing its border far to the west.

events.text: Annexation of the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania
events.detail: Using the secret protocol, the Soviet Union expanded further. It invaded Finland on 30 November 1939; the Finns resisted fiercely in the Winter War, but by the Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940 they ceded the Karelian Isthmus, Ladoga Karelia and other areas. In June 1940 Soviet troops occupied Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which were annexed as Soviet republics in August; most Western countries never recognised this. Between 28 June and 3 July 1940, after an ultimatum, the Soviets also occupied Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina from Romania. The USSR now reached the Baltic coast and the Danube delta.

events.text: Germany invades the Soviet Union on 22 June
events.detail: On 22 June 1941 Germany broke the pact and launched Operation Barbarossa, invading the Soviet Union with more than 3.8 million Axis troops along a front of about 2,900 kilometres. Soviet forces were caught largely unprepared, and in the first months the Germans encircled and captured whole armies and overran the Baltic states, Belarus and much of Ukraine, before they were stopped in the Battle of Moscow in late 1941. The Axis deliberately killed 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war and millions of civilians. The war on the Eastern Front, the largest theatre of the Second World War, killed over 26 million Soviet people.

events.text: German 6th Army surrenders at Stalingrad
events.detail: In the summer of 1942 the German army advanced towards the Volga River and the Caucasus oil fields, and in July it began its assault on Stalingrad, the city bearing Stalin's name. After months of brutal street fighting, a Soviet counter-offensive, Operation Uranus, launched on 19 November 1942, encircled the German 6th Army under Friedrich Paulus. Relief attempts and airlifts failed, and on 2 February 1943 the starving 6th Army capitulated. Stalingrad is generally regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe: the Soviets took the strategic initiative and began to drive the Germans back west.

events.text: Victory over Germany and Japan; southern Sakhalin and Kurils annexed
events.detail: After years of fighting, Soviet forces drove the Germans out of the Soviet Union and advanced through Eastern Europe, taking Berlin in May 1945; Germany surrendered on 8–9 May. As agreed with the Allies at Yalta, the Soviet Union then declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945 and invaded Manchuria, northern Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands. The USSR annexed southern Sakhalin and the Kurils, as well as eastern Poland, the Baltic states and other lands, and Soviet-backed communist governments were soon installed across Eastern Europe. The Soviet Union emerged as one of two global superpowers.

events.text: Death of Stalin
events.detail: Joseph Stalin, who had ruled the Soviet Union for about a quarter of a century, died on 5 March 1953 at his dacha at Kuntsevo after a stroke, aged 74. Millions had died in his purges, labour camps and famines, but he was mourned at a huge state funeral on 9 March. His inner circle, including Georgy Malenkov, Lavrentiy Beria and Nikita Khrushchev, competed to succeed him, and Khrushchev emerged as leader. Khrushchev went on to denounce his predecessor and launched a campaign of de-Stalinisation, freeing many political prisoners in what became known as the 'Khrushchev thaw'.

events.text: Soviet intervention in Afghanistan (withdrawal 1989)
events.detail: A communist government had seized power in Afghanistan in the Saur Revolution of 1978, but it faced a widespread rebellion; on 25 December 1979 Soviet troops entered the country, and its leader, Hafizullah Amin, was replaced by Babrak Karmal. The Soviet army spent nearly ten years fighting the mujahideen, guerrilla fighters backed mainly by Pakistan and the United States, along with Britain, China, Iran and Arab states. Between about 14,500 and 26,000 Soviet soldiers died, and far more Afghans. Gorbachev announced a withdrawal, and the last Soviet troops left on 15 February 1989. The costly war weakened the Soviet Union and damaged its standing in the world.

events.text: Gorbachev comes to power: glasnost and perestroika
events.detail: On 11 March 1985, after the death of the elderly Konstantin Chernenko, the Communist Party chose 54-year-old Mikhail Gorbachev as its General Secretary. Facing a stagnant economy and an expensive arms race, he launched glasnost ('openness'), allowing more freedom of speech and of the press, and perestroika ('restructuring'), which tried to decentralise economic decision-making. He also held summits with US President Ronald Reagan to limit nuclear weapons and began withdrawing from Afghanistan. His reforms unleashed forces he could not control, including nationalist movements in the Soviet republics.

events.text: Soviet-backed regimes fall across Eastern Europe
events.detail: Gorbachev made clear that the Soviet Union would no longer intervene to prop up communist governments in its Eastern European satellites, a policy jokingly called the 'Sinatra Doctrine'. In Poland the Solidarity movement won a landslide in elections on 4 June 1989, and a non-communist government took office. Over the following months communist regimes fell in Hungary, East Germany, where the Berlin Wall was opened in November, Czechoslovakia in the Velvet Revolution, Bulgaria and, violently, Romania. By the end of 1989 the Soviet bloc in Eastern Europe had collapsed, ending the Soviet Union's empire beyond its borders.

events.text: Failed August coup; the USSR is dissolved on 26 December
events.detail: On 19 August 1991 hardline communists, including the defence minister and the KGB chief, tried to seize power, placing Gorbachev under house arrest in Crimea. Crowds led by Boris Yeltsin, president of the Russian republic, defended the parliament building in Moscow, and the coup collapsed within days. The republics rushed to declare independence. On 8 December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the Belovezha Accords declaring that the Soviet Union no longer existed, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned. On 26 December 1991 the USSR was formally dissolved into 15 independent states, with Russia as its successor.
